Exertional fatigue, sleep restriction, and underfeeding are common stressors during sustained operations and together impair a Soldier's ability to maintain thermal balance in the cold. Some of the most common nonfreezing cold-weather injuries are described in paragraphs 3-57 through 3-75. Hypothermia 3-57. Hypothermia is the lowering of the body core temperature at a rate faster than the body can produce heat. Hypothermia may be caused by exposure or by sudden wetting of the body, such as falling into a lake or being sprayed with fuel or other liquid. Hypothermia can occur even on moderate days with temperatures of 40°F to 50°F with little precipitation if heat loss exceeds heat gain, and the Soldier's condition can deteriorate. Hypothermia is classified as mild (core temperature above 90°F or 32°Celsius [C]) or severe (core temperature below 90°F or 32°C). Eating sugary foods and physical activity helps to produce body heat. Treatment 3-63. Treatment methods vary based on the severity of the hypothermia. Mild cases-if Soldiers show symptoms of hypothermia, prevent additional heat loss by getting them into a shelter, if available; removing wet clothing; and replacing it with dry, insulated clothing. Extended training exercises test the sustainment mechanisms in place for the unit and expose the Soldier to the isolation common to mountain operations. SECTION II - COLD-WEATHER SUSTAINMENT 4-29. The ability to operate for extended periods in cold weather is an essential skill if a unit wishes to be successful in mountainous terrain. Chapter 4 accomplish its mission in cold, unforgiving weather, it must have the equipment necessary to live and operate in extreme conditions. Cold weather can affect many facets of daily life, from nutrition to clothing. CLOTHING 4-30. The clothing system refers to every piece of clothing placed against the skin (base layer), the insulating layers, and the outermost garments (shell), which protect the Soldier from the elements. When clothing is worn properly, the Soldier can function better; when clothing is worn improperly, Soldiers can develop hypothermia or frostbite. Wearing cold-weather clothing provides a barrier against weather and heat retention, moves moisture away from skin, dries quickly, and allows for adequate dexterity. 4-31. Clothing for the cold-weather environment must manage Soldiers' temperatures and control moisture. Clothing must be able to vent and breathe so a Soldier does not become overheated and perspire excessively. The clothing must also create insulation to shelter the Soldier from extreme temperatures. Clothing must manage moisture that comes from external sources, such as rain, or from internal sources, such as perspiration. 4-32. comes from external sources, such as rain, or from internal sources, such as perspiration. 4-32. One of the most effective ways to manage moisture from perspiration is to set a pace that limits exertion. In a cold-weather environment, patrols should move at a pace that will not saturate Soldiers' insulating layers with sweat. Rest halts allow Soldiers an opportunity to adjust layers and control their own individual temperatures. 4-33. Fitness, load, body composition, and metabolism all affect individual clothing needs. There should be room for individual variation in the wear of cold-weather clothing, but clothing decisions should be based on the principles of moisture management, trapped air spaces, and protection from the elements. The components of any clothing system can be broken down into the following general categories to match those principles. BASE LAYER 4-34. The base layer is a thin, lightweight moisture-wicking layer worn against skin and moves moisture away from the skin to prevent heat loss from conduction. Base layers should be constructed of wool, synthetic, or silk fabrics. INSULATING LAYERS 4-35. Insulating layers are those layers worn over the base layer and under the shell. Insulating layers provide additional warmth by resisting the transfer of heat. Modern

Base layers should be constructed of wool, synthetic, or silk fabrics. INSULATING LAYERS 4-35. Insulating layers are those layers worn over the base layer and under the shell. Insulating layers provide additional warmth by resisting the transfer of heat. Modern insulating layers allow moisture to move easily, and they trap air to increase the insulating factor. Several thin layers of insulation provide more warmth than one thick layer. Insulating layers should be constructed from wool, synthetic, or down fabrics. Insulating layers help Soldiers retain heat and not lose heat through convection. SHELL 4-36. The shell is the outermost layer worn. The shell is the primary barrier between the elements and the body and prevents outside moisture from getting in, while allowing inside moisture out. Shells must have some ventilation capacity to prevent overheating. There are two types of shells. 4-37. A hard shell is generally more moisture and wind repellant and provides better protection against the elements at the cost of breathability. Soldiers cannot ventilate their bodies as well with a hard shell. The hard shell is a good outer layer to be worn in extreme conditions or static environments. 4-38. The infective cysts and oocysts of protozoa are extremely robust and can survive for months in a water source. They thrive in domestic and wild animals, as well as humans. Chapter 5 Avalanche World War I is remembered for the brutal fighting in the trenches in France and Belgium. However, in the fighting between Italy and the Austro-Hungarian Empire, Soldiers saw some of the most intense mountain fighting in human history. After the Italians checked the Austrian offensive through the passes of the Alps, both sides fought higher and higher into the mountains. Small, light units of mountaineers clashed over new ground high in the peaks, while the armies dug in on the peaks they had secured. Positions and paths were blasted out of the rock and carved through the glaciers to move personnel and materiel to the fighting in the heights. By the winter of 1916, the line had mostly stabilized, and both armies were hunkering down for winter. Both sides had established extensive networks of trails and camps to support their forward positions; however, much of the infrastructure had been built in avalanche paths. In the second week of December, a major snowstorm blew in, loading the slopes and causing massive avalanches across the range. Both nations suppressed the number of casualties they received, and no official Italian records exist, but what evidence did survive paints a grim

of December, a major snowstorm blew in, loading the slopes and causing massive avalanches across the range. Both nations suppressed the number of casualties they received, and no official Italian records exist, but what evidence did survive paints a grim picture. The lowest estimates place casualties at around 4,000 during the storm. Some records support numbers as high as 10,000. Today, their bodies are still melting out of the glaciers below. SECTION I - AVALANCHE HAZARDS 5-1. During winter months and throughout the year, snow covers the slopes. Steep, snow-covered terrain, in addition to mobility challenges and fall hazards, present the risk of avalanches. This hazard is easy to underestimate. It is not clearly visible, and, due to the complexity of the factors involved, there is a high degree of uncertainty, but the consequences of ignoring the hazard are high. Avalanches have taken the lives of more troops engaged in mountain warfare than all other terrain hazards combined. 5-2. An avalanche is an unstable snowpack, located on particularly angled terrain, where the bonds between layers or several layers of snow have broken, causing a mass of snow to slide downhill. When operating in the mountains during the winter, these instabilities

avalanche is an unstable snowpack, located on particularly angled terrain, where the bonds between layers or several layers of snow have broken, causing a mass of snow to slide downhill. When operating in the mountains during the winter, these instabilities in the snowpack may make large areas too dangerous for travel. These snow slopes may appear unthreatening but may have weak layers buried in the snowpack that can be easily triggered. Military elements may gravitate into avalanche terrain to avoid steeper technical terrain or enemy observation. Avalanches can generate incredible destructive force, destroying equipment, killing or burying Soldiers, and blocking key roads. Whether operating dismounted in high alpine terrain or as a mounted force in valley bottoms, units must be aware of avalanche hazards. They must incorporate the evaluation of avalanche danger into the planning process and learn to recognize and avoid hazardous terrain. (See figure 5-1, page 64.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 63

Chapter 5 Figure 5-1. Movement through avalanche terrain AVALANCHE ELEMENTS 5-3. Avalanches occur when the weight of accumulated snow on a slope exceeds the cohesive forces that hold the snow in place. There are three elements needed to create an avalanche: an unstable snowpack, terrain steep enough to slide, and a trigger that initiates the failure of bonds holding the snow in place. SNOWPACK 5-4. Layers of snow accumulate with each new snow or wind event. Variation in temperature and atmospheric conditions form layers with different types of snow crystals. These layers are subject to changes in texture and strength throughout the winter, as they are exposed to sun, wind, and temperature changes. Each layer in the snowpack will have distinct characteristics. Strong layers are made up of well-bonded, small, rounded grains. Weak layers are made up of larger, angular, poorly bonded grains. Snowpack Concerns 5-5. Instabilities are weaknesses within the snowpack as described below (see figure 5-2): * Weak layers-weak layers may collapse under load, initiating an avalanche. Poorly bonded crystals can act like ball bearings between stronger layers. Weak layers can change over time, becoming stronger, denser layers. This happens more quickly in temperatures above freezing. However, many

Weak layers can change over time, becoming stronger, denser layers. This happens more quickly in temperatures above freezing. However, many avalanche cycles are due to weak layers that resist this change and retain their large grain size and 64 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Bed surface-the bed surface is the surface over which a fracture and subsequent avalanche release occurs. Smooth, uniform sliding surfaces provide less friction to hold the snow in place. A loose-dry avalanche is a release of dry, unconsolidated snow. These avalanches occur within layers of soft snow near the surface of the snowpack. Loose-dry avalanches start at a point and entrain snow as they move downhill, forming a fan-shaped avalanche. Other names for loose-dry avalanches include point-release avalanches or sluffs. Loose-dry avalanches can trigger slab avalanches that break into deeper snow layers. Avalanche SECTION III - AVALANCHE SEARCH AND RESCUE 5-40. The primary risk mitigation tool in avalanche terrain is avoidance. In the planning phase, Soldiers should make every effort to patrol routes that avoid avalanche hazards. The planning phase includes having clear decision points from which to evaluate conditions and viable alternate routes. However, when evaluating an avalanche hazard, there is often a high degree of uncertainty. When mistakes are made, the consequences are high. Avalanches produce incredible energy. Soldiers caught in an avalanche may be injured or killed by blunt force trauma from collisions with rock, ice, and trees. If they come to rest with an intact air pocket, they may succumb to hypothermia or shock. However, most avalanche victims die from asphyxiation. Without an air pocket, unconsciousness may come in minutes, followed rapidly by permeant brain injury and death. Evidence has shown that after 15 minutes, the chances of surviving complete burial decreases from 90 percent to 30 percent. It is critical that all Soldiers operating in avalanche terrain are equipped with avalanche safety equipment and are drilled in companion rescue. AVALANCHE SEARCH 5-41. Chapter 6 Mountain Mobility A unit's ability to maneuver through difficult and hazardous terrain provides it with access to the most tactically advantageous areas in the mountains. Units with Soldiers trained to a high level of mobility can move further, faster, and more safely through all levels of terrain. Mobility skill is the primary tool to manage risk when there is a fall hazard. Rope systems and belays can be used to mitigate fall risk during movement but require more time to complete, more technical training to accomplish, and can result in increased exposure to enemy attack. By far, the greatest combat multiplier in the mountains is high mobility skill. Units anticipating combat operations should focus on building individual movement skills over nearly all other special technical or tactical skills. SECTION I - INDIVIDUAL MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES 6-1. The speed at which the unit can move, the complexity of terrain they can negotiate unroped, and the violence of action they can muster as a team on the objective are all determined by the mobility of the unit's weakest members. Properly equipped units with mobility skills are more likely to outmaneuver the enemy in physically demanding and hazardous terrain. Soldiers who have been trained in mobility techniques can take advantage of terrain above operational level 2. This provides commanders with access to the highest and most difficult to reach points of domination in their areas of operation. For those untrained in mountaineering, such terrain can prove too hazardous to move in. However, units well-trained to maneuver here can take advantage of reduced combat risks during all types of combat operations by owning ground that most enemy forces cannot access, granting them overwhelming tactical advantage. As a result, individual mobility skills training should always be a high priority for units anticipating these operations. MOBILITY 6-2. Individual mobility comprises many factors, the most important of which are fitness and movement techniques. Soldiers can increase their mobility by practicing the movement techniques specific to negotiating rough terrain. Soldiers build proficiency by approaching movement from a skill-building perspective, whether the movement is walking, scrambling, or climbing, and regardless of whether the surface is dirt, rock, snow, or ice. The hallmarks of mobility are balance, surefootedness, and net endurance. The results are reduced likelihood of slipping or falling, reduced energy expended, increased speed, and the ability to focus on other critical tasks. A reasonable goal for Soldiers is the ability to move confidently through 3rd-class terrain unroped, even when exposed to fall hazards that would result in significant injury or death. BALANCE 6-3. Quality footwear, such as mountaineering boots, reduces many risks associated with moving in mountainous terrain. Quality boots increase both mobility and security of footing and can reduce orthopedic injuries. Boots designed for mountaineering range in weight, breathability, flexibility, and in how well they interface with other equipment. The rand helps protect the toe area from sharp rock and standing water. They have a high enough upper boot to protect the wearer's ankles from sharp rock and provide joint support against rolling. They have recessed soles made of softer rubber, a protective band around the forefoot, at least a partial shank, and are constructed with abrasion and water-resistant materials. Grassy slopes are usually composed of small tussocks of growth rather than one continuous field. When ascending, step on the upper side of each hummock or tussock, where the ground is more level. When descending a grassy slope, climbers should use the traverse technique because of the uneven nature of the ground. A climber can easily build up too much speed and fall if a direct descent is attempted. When traversing, the climber's uphill foot points in the direction of travel. The downhill foot points about 45° off the direction of travel (downhill). This maintains maximum sole contact and prevents possible downhill ankle rollout. MOUNTAIN WALKING 6-22. Mountain Mobility 6-24. General techniques for ascending: * As terrain becomes steeper, routes should adopt a traversing or switchback pattern. This involves moving diagonally up and across a slope, then turning back and doing the same in the opposite direction as necessary. This switchback pattern reduces the intensity and demand on large muscle groups, slows the onset of fatigue, and allows Soldiers to maintain situational awareness. Charging in a straight line up a steep hill is more demanding, results in more extreme fatigue and longer recovery time, and increases the likelihood of slips, falls, and injury. This technique should be avoided unless speed is critical, and all members of the group are highly fit and experienced moving this way. * The rest step technique involves locking out the rear leg briefly with each step. This gives muscles a micro rest with each step and results in greater endurance over long movements. (See figure 6-2, page 88.) * Pressure breathing-this technique involves breathing all the way out on the exhale to empty the lungs of air. This does two positive things. First, it ensures all carbon dioxide is pushed out of the lungs, reducing the likelihood of cramping, and making more

involves breathing all the way out on the exhale to empty the lungs of air. This does two positive things. First, it ensures all carbon dioxide is pushed out of the lungs, reducing the likelihood of cramping, and making more space for oxygenated air. Brush is both a help and a hindrance. Brush-filled gullies can provide routes and rally points concealed from observation; on the other hand, steep, brushy terrain is hazardous to negotiate. Cliffs and steep ravines are hidden traps, and blow downs and thickets can obstruct travel as much as manmade obstacles. Hard ground is firmly compacted, rocky soil that does not give way under the weight of a Soldier's step. It is usually found under mature forest canopy, in low brush or heather, and areas where animals have beaten out multiple trails. When ascending, employ the rest step to rest the leg muscles. 6-31. Scree fields are comprised of loose rock approximately fist-sized or smaller, that are common in the mountains and are a challenge to ascend. The experience is like climbing sand, except that the loose rock can be rough on ankles and lower legs. Climbers should avoid ascending scree fields, if

or smaller, that are common in the mountains and are a challenge to ascend. The experience is like climbing sand, except that the loose rock can be rough on ankles and lower legs. Climbers should avoid ascending scree fields, if possible, as they demand the expenditure of much more energy than other surfaces. Soldiers should kick in with the toe of the upper foot so that a step is formed in the loose scree. After determining that the step is stable, the Soldier transfers weight to the upper leg, then steps up, and repeats the process with the lower foot. The best method for descending scree slopes is to come straight down the slope using a short shuffling step with the knees bent, back straight, feet pointed downhill, and heels dug in. Chapter 6 SCRAMBLING 6-33. Scrambling is the act of moving over difficult or broken terrain, characterized by using mostly walking techniques but requires some use of the hands for balance or other specific climbing techniques. It is perhaps the most dangerous means of mobility in which snow and ice are not present. At the lowest level, scrambling involves simply placing a hand or hands on features periodically to help maintain balance and improve efficiency during movement. At the higher level, scrambling involves Soldiers making multiple easy rock-climbing moves, followed by several steps walking, and repeating that sequence throughout an ascent. 6-34. Typically, 3rd-class terrain is where Soldiers begin scrambling, but just exactly what terrain and terrain features require is determined largely by the mobility skill of the individual Soldier. Soldiers with low-mobility skill will need to use hands more often, especially if a fall risk is present, which will slow their movement. Soldiers with higher mobility skills need to use their hands less often for balance enabling them to move faster even when a fall risk is present. 6-35. The higher the rock-climbing skill, the more quickly, efficiently, and safely Soldiers can scramble. The best way to train Soldiers to

their hands less often for balance enabling them to move faster even when a fall risk is present. 6-35. The higher the rock-climbing skill, the more quickly, efficiently, and safely Soldiers can scramble. The best way to train Soldiers to be better at scrambling is to provide rock-climbing training. Rock climbing is easier to protect with ropes and forces Soldiers to use better movement techniques even though rock-climbing training involves steeper and more difficult terrain. SCRAMBLING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS 6-36. Scrambling terrain can be some of the most dangerous terrain through which Soldiers can move. Often it is the low ground between higher terrain features or cliffs, subjecting it to falling object hazards and significant tactical disadvantage. Additionally, it can be exposed to fall hazards below. 6-37. Good reconnaissance and route planning are critical for movements through scrambling terrain. Whenever possible, small teams of advanced military mountaineers should be sent to find the best route ahead of the main body. 6-38. Small teams may need to be sent forward to clear points of domination over the route. Sniper or machine gun overwatch positions may need to be established to cover movement through sections of terrain that is particularly exposed to enemy attack. All these security measures increase movement times significantly. (See ATP 3-21.50 for VDA-crossing TTP.) 6-39. Two-point slings should be used to secure rifles close to the body. Heavier weapon systems, such as sniper rifles and machine guns, may need to be secured to rucksacks close to the body during sustained scrambling to allow Soldiers to use their hands freely for assistance. Possessing rock-climbing skills (discussed later in the chapter) increases the efficiency with which Soldiers can scramble. Vegetation may appear to provide good handholds but may easily pull free. The probability and consequence of falls are high, even under the best conditions. Rope systems are usually necessary to protect climbers from injury or death, slowing movement and reducing tactical maneuverability. 6-42. Building rock-climbing skill increases the confidence and speed at which Soldiers can move unroped in easier terrain, even when subjected to higher fall consequence. The basic principles of rock climbing are the same as walking in rough terrain; they are just more difficult to achieve, and the required movements less intuitive. ROCK CLIMBING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS 6-47. Sustained climbing in 5th-class terrain during conventional military operations is impractical. However, routes through easier terrain are often blocked by shorter sections of 4th or easier 5th-class terrain. These routes may be the only or most tactically sound approaches to points of domination for properly trained units. Small teams of advanced military mountaineers can be used to establish fixed-rope routes for lesser-trained Soldiers to use for protection during movement. Accessing these points may be required to reach enemy defensive positions, establish observation posts, or position small teams conducting reconnaissance or forward observation of fires. 6-48. Before climbing, Soldiers should scan the rock for features that indicate that climbing the route is possible. With experience, Soldiers can determine how difficult a section of rock will be for them to complete. 92 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

(See chapter 10 on how to protect climbers from fall hazards.) 6-50. During military operations, the least difficult routes possible should be selected for travel. (See chapter 7 for more information on planning technical movement routes.) ROCK-CLIMBING TECHNIQUES 6-51. The basic principles for rock climbing are the same as those for walking in rough terrain. They are finding and selecting suitable holds and positioning the body to achieve sufficient friction for continued movement. Due to the vertical nature of the terrain, hands must be used to aid Soldiers in maintaining balance and preventing them from tipping backward off the rock. 6-52. Suspect rock-climbing holds should be tested to ensure they are secure by tapping with a hand or foot. Holds that move or shift should be avoided. This is common in undeveloped 4th- and 5th-class terrain. Maintaining Balance 6-53. Balance is the most important aspect of rock climbing and footwork is the foundation of balance. Good use of the feet saves energy and makes staying in balance easier. A relaxed, comfortable

undeveloped 4th- and 5th-class terrain. Maintaining Balance 6-53. Balance is the most important aspect of rock climbing and footwork is the foundation of balance. Good use of the feet saves energy and makes staying in balance easier. A relaxed, comfortable stance is essential. The body should be centered over the feet as much as possible. On lower angle sections of climbing, it should be positioned away from the rock face. Alternatively, it should be positioned closer to the rock face on steeper sections. This puts downward pressure on footholds, increasing their security. Smaller lower body movements are often less strenuous than larger ones, which take more effort to stay in balance. 6-54. Rock climbing usually requires the use of handholds to maintain balance. Handholds can be large jugs that allow climbers to hold nearly their whole weight or tiny crimpers that only hold a fraction of their weight. Specific handhold techniques are discussed throughout this section. New climbers commonly overuse their arms to pull themselves up the rock and burn out quickly. Tired or pumped forearms are a sign of bad footwork. 6-55. Whenever possible, three points of contact should be maintained while moving the fourth to the next hold.

their arms to pull themselves up the rock and burn out quickly. Tired or pumped forearms are a sign of bad footwork. 6-55. Whenever possible, three points of contact should be maintained while moving the fourth to the next hold. This can reduce the likelihood of a fall should one point of contact fail. Types of Contact 6-56. Though counterintuitive, often pushing rather than pulling is required during climbing. Using downward pressure involves pushing down on a feature with the hands to allow unweighting of the other hand or one foot for movement to the next hold. Using counterpressure involves pushing away from features to allow a hand or foot to be unweighted for movement. (See figure 6-5, page 94.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 93

Chapter 6 Figure 6-5. Downward or counterpressure 6-57. Occasionally, the holds available put the climber out of balance, but repositioning the body (usually by extending a leg to the left or right) improves the climber's balance. This technique is called counterbalancing and often allows the climber greater reach. (See figure 6-6.) Often the climber can find a microfeature to touch or apply slight pressure to with the foot improving the security of the move. 94 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-6. Counterbalance 6-58. Occasionally, the climber must switch hands or feet on a hold to make the next move. Sometimes the hold can be shared temporarily by two hands or feet, even if they are unsecure, while the lead hand or lead foot moves. Other times, the second hand or foot may need to use a temporary, perhaps less desirable hold, while the lead one moves. 6-59. Dynamic moves are sudden, explosive moves where climbers throw themselves out of balance, potentially even losing contact with the rock, to reach another hold. These moves must be calculated carefully because failing to execute them perfectly usually results in a fall. Slab and Face Climbing 6-60. Slabs are typically smoother, lower angle rock features. They can be large or small. Comparatively, they provide the climber with few hands and footholds and require good footwork and balancing to climb. The primary technique used to climb them is smearing with the feet. This involves placing the sole of the boot or shoe on the rock with toe facing uphill to obtain maximum contact and friction. The body is then positioned away from the rock so that the foot does not slip. The

This involves placing the sole of the boot or shoe on the rock with toe facing uphill to obtain maximum contact and friction. The body is then positioned away from the rock so that the foot does not slip. The closer climbers can get to pushing perpendicular to the rock, the more friction they will create. (See figure 6-7, page 96.) Hands are usually used to help balance by pushing against the rock. Any microfeature that can be found will improve the security of climbing slabby terrain. Climbing slabby rock helps build confidence in footwork and good balance skills. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 95

Chapter 6 6-61. Face climbing is what is commonly associated with rock climbing. Face climbs are typically suitably featured rock faces (cliffs) where climbers employ a wide variety of basic moves to ascending. Climbers spend most of their time facing the rock, like climbing a ladder. Many footholds are small or sloped and require edging or smearing to be effective; others are larger. (See figure 6-8.) Many techniques for using handholds exist. (See figure 6-8.) Using knees should be avoided because they are more likely to slip than good footwear. 6-62. Most slab or face climbing terrain appropriate to military operations can be climbed in combat boots, mountaineering boots, or approach shoes. Moderate to difficult climbs require climbing shoes. (See figure 6-9.) Figure 6-7. Footholds Figure 6-8. Handhold techniques 96 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-9. Slab body position Resting During Climbing 6-63. Resting is critical during sustained rock climbing. Any opportunity to stand up and let go or lightly hold on with the hands should be taken. Sometimes the body or a body part can be wedged into a large crack, allowing the climber to relax. Often, the only rests available are between moves while looking for the next hold. When not actively moving, climbers should keep their weight on their skeletal system as much as possible. This means locking out legs or arms and providing muscles with a brief rest. Doing this is particularly important to preserve arm strength. Often one arm and the climbers' feet can support their weight while they shake out the other arm and hand. (See figure 6-10, page 98.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 97

Chapter 6 Figure 6-10. Rest or shake out Specific Moves 6-64. Mantling involves pulling down with both arms on the edge of a ledge type feature until the chest is ledge height, then transitioning to pushing down on the ledge while walking the feet up the face below. This move is common to climbing out of a swimming pool. (See figure 6-11.) 98 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility 6-65. Stemming involves placing the feet on features to the left and right of the body so that force is applied outward as well as down. Stemming is typically very stable and requires a relatively low amount of energy to maintain. (See figure 6-12, page 100.) 6-66. Underclinging involves gripping an overhanging rock feature with the hands, palm up, and pushing against a lower rock face with the feet. Underclings can be very stable but can be quite strenuous and tiring. Occasionally, underlings are the only means of getting through a section of climbing. (See figure 6-13, page 101.) 6-67. Liebacking involves using counterforce by pulling hard on a vertical or diagonal feature (such as a large flake) while pushing hard against the face of the rock. These moves are very strenuous because little or none of the climbers' weights is supported by their feet. In fact, leg muscles are being used to push away from the rock, so they are very taxing to the upper body. The climber's hands are then walked up the feature while the feet are walked up the face. Chapter 6 Figure 6-14. Liebacking Crack Climbing 6-68. Crack climbing requires a specific set of nonintuitive techniques that take quite a bit of practice to build proficiency in. While some climbs involving cracks can be climbed with weak or no crack technique, more difficult crack climbs require climbing shoes and good technique to be climbable. Mixed crack climbing involves using features on the rock face for footholds while using a prominent crack for handholds. (See figure 6-15.) Classic crack climbing involves moving up a prominent crack by alternately jamming hands or fingers and feet or toes and walking them up the crack. Often, one foot is placed out of the crack to the side for balance, even on a featureless face. Off-width crack climbing is the term for climbing cracks that are larger than fist and foot sized but not large enough to fit the entire body. These climbs are difficult. 102 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-15. Mixed face and crack climbing Jamming 6-69. A critical technique in climbing cracks involves placing a hand or foot into a crack and turning, twisting, or otherwise manipulating them so that they become temporarily jammed in the crack. A good jam can be achieved in a variety of ways depending on crack size, whether it has constrictions in it or not, and its position in relation to other holds on the climb. Jams can provide solid hands or footholds but are often uncomfortable or even painful. Crack size determines which jam technique to use for a given hold. Constrictions in the crack make jam holds more secure. Types of Hand Jams 6-70. Hand-sized jams are the easiest to perform. The hand is inserted open into the crack and then the fingers bent exert pressure against the walls of the crack. Often turning one hand thumb down is useful. Typically, leaning to the same side adds security to a thumb up hand jam. (See figure 6-16, page 104 for variations of hand jamming.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 103

Chapter 6 6-71. Fist jams are techniques necessary for cracks that are larger than those that work for hand jams. The same jamming principles apply, but climbers just insert their entire fist into the crack. (See figure 6-17 for variations of fist jamming.) 6-72. Finger jams are techniques necessary for cracks that are smaller than those that will accept a hand. The same jamming principles apply, but the climber only inserts their fingers, or parts of their fingers into the crack. Finger jamming is more difficult and can be painful for the joints. It is important to strengthen finger muscles prior to attempting to support substantial weight with finger jams to prevent joint strain. (See figure 6-18.) Types of Foot Jams 6-73. Foot jams involve turning the foot so that it fits into the crack and then twisting it so that the width of the foot wedges into the crack. This can be uncomfortable but can provide very secure footholds. (See figure 6-19.) 6-74. Toe jams are used in the same manner as foot jams, but in smaller cracks. (See figure 6-20, page 106.) Chicken wing is a technique also used for off-width cracks and involves inserting an entire arm into the crack bent at the elbow and pushing against one wall of the crack with the hand to create a jam. Climbing dihedrals and chimneys involves positioning the body inside a feature and using counterpressure or stemming to make upward movement. These features can often make for less strenuous climbing due to the counterpressure positions allowing for more rests. A dihedral is two rock faces that meet to form a corner, like an open book. Often there is a crack where the two faces meet. Chimneys are roughly parallel-sided features. They could be like a vertical shaft or crack large enough to accept a whole body. 6-78. Dihedrals can usually be climbed with a combination of stemming and either crack or face climbing. Dihedrals are easier and less strenuous to climb when the two faces have multiple and large features. 6-79. Chimneys are often unpleasant features to climb but provide a lot of security during movement. The basic technique for climbers is to position their body in the chimney and use counterpressure by pushing with arms, legs, and back against opposing sides. This is often necessary because the features that make up a rock route are not always continuous or travel straight up a face. Traversing often involves a series of placement exchanges. Most traversing is done facing the rock. 6-81. Hand traversing requires a ledge, flake, other horizontal feature, or a series of horizontally oriented large handholds. Climbers' hands walk their way across the features while their feet walk their way across a face below. (See figure 6-25, page 110.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 109

Chapter 6 6-82. Steep traverse is a technique often used when handholds are not as good, but decent footholds are present. Climbers lean heavily in the direction they want to move and place hands on available holds, and then walk their feet in the same direction using available footholds. Sometimes a crossover step is helpful. This technique typically requires solid side pulling, counterpressure, and counterforce skills. (See figure 6-26.) Figure 6-25. Hand traverse Topping Out or Gaining Ledges 6-83. Topping out or gaining a ledge can be one of the more challenging parts of climbing. Often low holds located near where climbers want to put their feet need to be used to get over the edge. Often, a mantling technique is effective. Most importantly, climbers should avoid laying on their belly on the edge when moving because it may be difficult to get their feel back on the rock, and they may slide off on sloped ledges. A crossover step is helpful. This technique typically requires solid side pulling, counterpressure, and counterforce skills. (See figure 6-26 for the proper technique.) 110 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

This is largely because rock features are often difficult to identify from above. They are easily obscured by other features above them or even the climber's body parts. However, down climbing is an important skill to practice, as it is often necessary to do in 3rd- and 4th-class terrain. 6-85. Facing out is a technique used on low angle rock. Climbers face out and use their hands for stability behind and below their body while moving their feet down to the next hold. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 6-86. Walking down a slab is a technique that involves simply walking down slabby rock while maintaining maximum friction and balance. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 6-87. Facing sideways involves climbers facing to the side and side stepping down to lower footholds while controlling and balancing their movement using handholds above. Climbers use this technique on steeper rock. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 6-88. Facing the rock involves climbing down in the same position as the climber would use to move up the rock. Facing the rock involves climbing down in the same position as the climber would use to move up the rock. Climbers lower themselves down with their arms, keeping their body away from the rock so they can see footholds below, and then transition their weight onto the next foothold. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 111

Chapter 6 Figure 6-27. Down climbing TRAINING FOR ROCK CLIMBING 6-89. Beginner rock-climbing training is typically conducted at established climbing areas using top rope belay techniques (see chapter 10). When supervised by qualified mountaineers, this kind of rock climbing is relatively low risk and has a high payoff for developing mobility skills. One restriction is that sites do not often allow large groups to be actively engaged. Thus, climbing training should be planned along with concurrent training for smaller groups to rotate through. Route difficulty should be challenging to climbers but easy enough that they can be successful. This motivates climbers to build skills. A motivational rather than critical atmosphere is most effective when building climbing skills. 6-90. Climbing training for more advanced military mountaineers can be conducted the same way, just on more challenging routes, but should also be conducted in a multipitch setting that more accurately reproduces conditions of climbing during military operations. This setting requires the development of lead climbing and route-finding skills, which are critical to the advanced military mountaineer. 6-91. Leaders should try to learn the etiquette associated with climbing before using civilian climbing areas. 112 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility SECTION II - MOVEMENT OVER SNOW AND ICE 6-92. Deep snow, steep powdery slopes, glare ice, and frozen waterfalls all present significant challenges to movement. The basic individual movement principles and skill development necessary for movement under other surface conditions also apply to movement over snow and ice. However, additional skills are necessary for efficiency and safety. Specialized equipment is required in even the easiest snow or ice-covered terrain. MOBILITY OVER SNOW AND ICE 6-93. Fitness and movement techniques are the foundation of moving through snow or up steep ice. However, identifying and selecting secure foot placements can be difficult because traction is drastically reduced. Movement without specialized equipment, such as crampons or skis, is difficult under almost all conditions above 1st-class terrain. Even when it is possible, deep snow requires a substantial amount of energy to move through unaided. Anything deeper than calf-deep snow will impede movement in even easy terrain, and a few inches of snow or a glaze of ice will make steeper terrain treacherous. Soldiers must develop the same level of skill using snow and ice equipment, which requires proficiency in an additional set of skills. Like moving over broken rocky terrain, these skills

or a glaze of ice will make steeper terrain treacherous. Soldiers must develop the same level of skill using snow and ice equipment, which requires proficiency in an additional set of skills. Like moving over broken rocky terrain, these skills can only be developed through experience and repetition. Units that train their Soldiers to proficiency in these conditions can move faster, safer, and access terrain that others cannot. EQUIPMENT FOR SNOW AND ICE 6-94. Skis provide substantial floatation in deep snow and require the least amount of energy for movement. This is especially true for downhill movement where much energy can be saved over walking. There are varieties of ski systems available for movement over snow, but those most suited to military mountaineering are called alpine touring skis. The ski itself is like a downhill ski, but the binding allows the heel to release for movement over flat or uphill terrain. It can also be locked down for greater control when skiing downhill. Climbing skins are used in conjunction with skis to climb uphill. Skins are designed to slide in only one direction, providing traction in deep snow and on steep slopes. At a minimum, a stiff mountaineering boot is

when skiing downhill. Climbing skins are used in conjunction with skis to climb uphill. Skins are designed to slide in only one direction, providing traction in deep snow and on steep slopes. At a minimum, a stiff mountaineering boot is necessary for use with skis. In the steepest terrain, a dedicated rigid plastic ski boot may be required. Compatibility between boots and bindings must be considered. (See figure 6-28, page 114.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 113

Chapter 6 Figure 6-28. Alpine touring skis 6-95. Snowshoes are another tool available to Soldiers for moving over deep snow. Modern snowshoes provide sufficient floatation and traction for moving through snow on fairly steep (class 2) slopes and should be small and light enough to pack, if necessary. Snowshoes work with any boot. (See figure 6-29.) 114 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-29. Snowshoes 6-96. Ski poles are typically used with snowshoes and skis to provide more lateral stability and balance. Ski poles can be used to provide excellent support for weapons systems during firing from the prone, kneeling, and standing positions. 6-97. Sleds are useful for carrying large amounts of equipment, such as bivouac equipment, heavy weapons, food and water, or other supplies. They range in size, shape, and weight, all of which should be considered before selection for military operations. Four- and ten-Soldier Ahkio-style sleds are available through the military supply system. These are designed to carry all group sustainment equipment (for example, tents, stoves, fuel) for a four- or ten-Soldier group. These come with a cover and rigid poles, convenient for dragging up and downhill. (See figure 6-30, page 116.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 115

Chapter 6 Figure 6-30. Ahkio sleds 6-98. Crampons attach to the Soldier's boot to provide traction on ice and snow. There are two basic types: general mountaineering crampons and ice climbing crampons. Mountaineering crampons have less aggressive points. They are designed for use in steep snow and on low-angle ice and can be used for ice climbing but are not ideal. Ice climbing crampons have points that are more aggressive and are typically more rigid. They are designed for steep ice climbing but can be used in snow and low angle ice as well. Crampons work best when paired with a stiff leather or rigid plastic mountaineering boot. They do not work well with issued cold-weather combat boots. (See figure 6-31.) Figure 6-31. Crampons 6-99. Mountain axes are important tools for movement over steep snow and occasional low-angle ice. The two types of axes usually used in alpine terrain are general mountain axes and hybrid mountain axes. General axes are designed for steep snow and hybrid axes are designed for steep snow and low-angle ice climbing. Ice axes have an adze to the rear of the pick for chopping snow and ice. Chapter 6 Figure 6-33. Ice tools MILITARY OPERATIONS IN SNOW- AND ICE-COVERED TERRAIN 6-101. Snow and ice present many additional challenges for units that need to move in mountainous terrain. Specialized equipment, training, and experience are necessary to move in it safely and effectively. Whether the challenges are deep snow, slick slopes, or steep sections of vertical ice, they will prove substantial obstacles for unprepared units. Units anticipating operating in such terrain and conditions should train in them prior to engaging in combat operations. 6-102. Even with proper equipment and training, it is unlikely that larger units can move in terrain steeper than 2nd-class terrain without ropes due to the high risk of long sliding falls. Small teams of advanced military mountaineers should be trained to move over ice and snow and tasked with finding routes and establishing rope systems for larger units. (See chapter 11 for establishing fixed-rope systems for troop movement in steep terrain and ATP 3-21.50 for crossing VDA TTP.) 118 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility MOVEMENT OVER SNOW 6-103. Low- to moderate-angle snow slopes found on or adjacent to valleys are primary avenues of movement for military units operating in winter conditions. Steeper slopes in gullies and passes are often the easiest routes through even steeper rocky features around them. Though challenging to move over, these often provide the best access to points of domination in alpine terrain. 6-104. Techniques for moving over snowy surfaces change IAW slope and surface conditions. Some soft snow increases physical strain but can increase the security of foot placements. During movement, breaks should be taken more frequently and for shorter durations in cold weather to assist with moisture management. This helps prevent overheating, which can cause problems once movements stop. Snow deeper than calf-height makes movement difficult without skis or snowshoes. Hard-packed snow slopes requiring special techniques and equipment or falls that could result in serious injury or death are likely. 6-105. A thorough analysis of avalanche threat should be conducted prior to moving over slopes that could be exposed to avalanche risk. Terrain at any risk for avalanche should be avoided. Chapter 6 Figure 6-34. Step cutting GLISSADING 6-108. Glissading is a technique used to descend low to moderate angle slopes by sliding in the seated position and using a mountain axe as a brake. (See figure 6-35.) Glissading allows Soldiers to descend appropriate slopes very quickly and efficiently, thereby saving significant time and energy. Specific conditions are required for glissading to be appropriate. The slope should not have any obstacles (such as trees, rocks, drop offs, crevasses) in the slide path, and it should have sufficient soft snow on the surface to allow Soldiers to control the speed of the slide. Glissading should never be done on hard-packed snow or ice surfaces. Crampons should be removed prior to glissading to ensure injuries to lower extremities are not caused by a crampon becoming caught on something during the slide. 6-109. Glissading is conducted by sitting in the snow and positioning the midpoint of a mountain axe shaft against one hip with the spike in the snow. The hand on the same side as the axe holds its shaft to the hip at the midpoint. The other hand holds the top of the axe where pick, shaft and adze meet. The mountain

the spike in the snow. The hand on the same side as the axe holds its shaft to the hip at the midpoint. The other hand holds the top of the axe where pick, shaft and adze meet. The mountain axe pick should always face forward (away from the Soldier) to prevent injury. Soldiers then initiate the slide on their buttocks using the axe spike as a brake. To slow down, Soldiers rotate the spike downward, pressing it deeper into the snowpack and increasing friction. To speed up, Soldiers rotate the spike away from the snowpack, decreasing friction. Adequate time should be allowed between Soldiers sliding in the same glissade path to ensure a collision does not occur should a Soldier stop shortly mid-slide. 120 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-35. Glissading FLATFOOTING 6-110. Flatfooting is the term for numerous techniques that increase security and efficiency of movement over snow and ice slopes. These techniques involve the use of both crampons and a mountain axe. The key principle of flatfooting is to position the body so that all crampon points are embedded in the snow surface. This provides maximum security for foot placements. These techniques are particularly critical to safe movement over steep, hard-packed snow. Flatfooting with heavy loads requires greater proficiency. Flatfooting techniques are much more difficult to perform in flexible boots or with loose sloppy crampons. (See figure 6-36, page 122.) 6-111. Crampons substantially increase the security of foot placements when used properly. However, walking in them forces the Soldier's gait to change and can take some practice getting used to. They must be sized properly and snugged tight to the boot, so Soldiers' boots do not slide around in the crampon introducing instability to their foot placements. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 121

Flatfooting, using a mountain axe in a cross-body position. To perform this technique, the Soldier stands sideways to the slope. The mountain axe head is held in the downhill hand and the shaft held low in the uphill hand. The uphill foot is placed perpendicular to the slope and the downhill foot is placed similarly, but with the toe pointed downhill as much as comfort demands. The axe spike is then forced into the snowpack uphill from the feet far enough so that most of the Soldier's weight is transitioned onto it. This provides balance and security during foot movement. Chapter 6 6-117. Front pointing involves kicking into the slope with the toe of the boot so that all front crampon points become embedded in the surface. The Soldier leans forward slightly locking the ankle so that the sole of the foot is held perpendicular to the slope. If the heel is too low or too high, or only the large front points are embedded, then the foot placement will be less secure and may fail. The Soldier stands up on the placement using hands or mountain axe for balance and repeats kicking in with the other foot higher on the slope. This process is repeated as the Soldier generally moves straight up the slope. The front-pointing technique is very effective and allows for faster movement in steep terrain but is more physically taxing. The Soldier's calf muscles become fatigued quickly using this technique. The front-pointing technique is most effective for ascending short, steep sections of terrain. (See figure 6-40.) Figure 6-40. Front pointing 6-118. Mountain Mobility Descending 6-121. Slips and slides should be considered very likely on moderate to steep terrain, especially if surface conditions are hard. Rope systems may be used to mitigate the risk of injury, but they do not make movement faster or easier. Efficient movement requires good flatfooting skills. 6-122. Moderately steep slopes can be descended by simply using a diagonal traverse or switchback pattern down the slope. This may require rolling the ankle more than usual to force all crampon points into the snow. The downhill foot can be turned so that the toe points downhill to reduce strain and add security during movement. The mountain axe is used in any of the positions described above to aid with balance and prepare the Soldier for self-arrest. Edging technique is ineffective; Solders should not attempt this technique. (See figure 6-44, page 128.) 6-123. Chapter 6 Figure 6-44. Descending steep slopes SELF-ARREST 6-127. Self-arrest is a technique intended to stop a short fall before it turns into a long, sliding, tumbling fall. Soldiers that will be moving on moderate to steep snow slopes unroped must be issued a mountain axe at a minimum and trained to proficiency in self-arrest techniques. There is little margin for error in executing self-arrest on steep slopes with firm surface conditions. Self-arresting should not be considered an adequate protective measure when slipping and falling risk is determined to be likely. Good movement skills are still the primary risk mitigation for moving unroped. 6-128. Soldiers should carry the axe in the cane position with the pick to the rear in the uphill hand. The instant Soldiers fall, they must commit to self-arresting immediately. The technique is executed by bringing the mountain axe into position at the center of chest, with the hand on its head and pick facing away. The lower hand moves to a position low on the axe shaft. The Soldier then uses body weight and violence of action to drive the pick into the snowpack. This must be done in seconds and if the axe is not

lower hand moves to a position low on the axe shaft. The Soldier then uses body weight and violence of action to drive the pick into the snowpack. This must be done in seconds and if the axe is not centered under the body, it is difficult to apply adequate force to achieve this. The less aggressive and curved design of the ice axe pick is meant to prevent it from biting into the surface too well, where momentum would cause it to be ripped out of the falling Soldiers' hands. Rather, it is designed to stop the Soldier gradually. For this reason, picks that are more aggressive like those found on tools meant for ice climbing are less effective for this. If crampons are not worn, the Soldier can also dig toes into the snowpack to assist stopping the slide. Careful attention must be paid not to allow the spike of the axe to dig into the snow while sliding. If this happens, the Soldier could be flipped over backwards and thrown into a tumble. To self-arrest while sliding on the back, the Soldier must bring the axe into position at the center of the chest, then roll in the direction of the axe head until on the stomach, and then drive the pick into the snow. 6-131. Ice climbing is demanding and requires specialized equipment and techniques. Waterfall ice develops in the bottom and along the steep sides of drainages, such as gullies and couloirs. (See figure 6-46.) Alpine ice can develop in the same areas or in glacial features that are more open. (See figure 6-47.) Mountain Mobility Figure 6-47. Alpine ice 6-137. All the hazards associated with rock climbing exist for ice climbing, as well as additional ones, including avalanches and icefalls. Icefall is always a real threat to ice climbers and personnel located below them. This is particularly true during warmer temperatures as hanging ice features can break off and fall naturally. Ice climbers are at higher risk of injury during a fall due to the sharp tools and crampons used in climbing. Even short falls can result in a tool accidentally puncturing the climber's body, or a crampon catching on a feature during the fall and causing lower extremity injuries. 6-138. Climbing ice usually requires the use of rope systems for protection even when climber's skills are high due to the consequences of falling. ICE CLIMBING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS 6-139. Sustained climbing in 5th-class terrain during conventional military operations is impractical, especially when covered in ice. However, routes through easier terrain are often blocked by short sections of low or steep angle waterfall ice. These routes may be the only or most tactically sound approaches to points of domination for properly trained units. Small teams of advanced mountaineers can be used to establish

blocked by short sections of low or steep angle waterfall ice. These routes may be the only or most tactically sound approaches to points of domination for properly trained units. Small teams of advanced mountaineers can be used to establish fixed-rope routes through this terrain for lesser-trained Soldiers to use for protection during movement. 6-140. Typically, Soldiers climbing ice are unable to provide themselves with sufficient, local security during movement. Bounding overwatch in vertical terrain by small-specialized teams or VDA-crossing procedures must be performed by a larger unit to provide adequate security for climbing Soldiers. (See ATP 3-21.50 for more on VDA crossing.) Chapter 6 ICE CLIMBING ROUTE SELECTION 6-141. Before starting to climb, Soldiers should study the face of the ice flow for features that indicate that climbing the route is possible. With experience, Soldiers can determine how difficult an ice flow will be for them to climb and how reliable protection placements will be. Climbers should form a plan for climbing and protection using rope systems (when necessary) before leaving the ground. (See chapter 10 for how to protect climbers from fall hazards.) 6-142. During military operations, the least difficult routes possible should be selected for travel. (See chapter 7 for more information on planning technical movement routes.) BASIC ICE CLIMBING TECHNIQUES 6-143. Compared to rock climbing, ice climbing movement techniques are relatively simple. The most difficult part is learning how to place tools and crampons into the ice so that they hold the climber's weight, and then moving in balance so as not to dislodge them or waste energy. The keys to efficient ice climbing are a reliable and secure tool, crampon placements, and staying in balance during movement. 6-144. Complicated movement techniques are rarely necessary in ice climbing. Using Ice Tools 6-145. The purpose of the tools in ice

keys to efficient ice climbing are a reliable and secure tool, crampon placements, and staying in balance during movement. 6-144. Complicated movement techniques are rarely necessary in ice climbing. Using Ice Tools 6-145. The purpose of the tools in ice climbing is to provide climbers with handholds to hang from while moving their feet and for maintaining balance while moving the body. Whenever possible, each tool placement should be secure enough to hold the climber's entire body weight. 6-146. Modern ice tools should be held loosely by the grip, with the heel of the hand wedged into the hook or stop at the bottom of the shaft. This feature allows the climber to hang without squeezing. When done properly, the climber's weight can be held with just moderate pressure from two or three fingers around the grip. (See figure 6-48.) 6-147. Some force must be used when swinging ice tools, but how they are swung is more important than how hard it is. Placing tools starts with positioning the climber's hips close to the ice creating space to swing the tool. This becomes more important as the ice gets steeper. The tool is swung in an overhead arc with a flick of the wrist as the pick is about to strike the ice. 6-148. Ideal tool placements are as high as the climber can comfortably reach and as close to the centerline of the body as possible. Ice tools can be removed from the ice by gently tapping upward on the adze or hammer to loosen the pick in the ice. Vertical ice or technical crampons are preferred, but not always necessary. 6-151. Crampon placements on low-angle ice are used in the same manner as flatfooting with occasional front pointing. The hard surface of the ice requires more effort to ensure crampon points are set securely in the ice before committing weight to them. Edging techniques are insecure on ice. 6-152. When using crampon placements on moderate and steeper ice flows, front pointing is used exclusively. Climbers must move their lower body away from the ice during crampon placement. Good front point placements are those in which all front points are in solid contact with the ice and the foot is perpendicular to the surface. (See figure 6-40, page 124.) Mountain Mobility Special Moves 6-157. Stemming is the same as in rock climbing and provides the same benefits. The opportunity to do this is created by a groove feature running vertically up and down the ice. Climbers kick their crampons diagonally into the sides of the feature for very secure foot placements. Stemming makes climbing steep ice much easier. 6-158. Climbing over ice bulges is challenging because maintaining a high tool for balance is not always possible. The high tool must be placed low in relation to the body on a horizontal feature. Feet must then walked up the lower face as close to the lip of the bulge as necessary for the climber to step onto the top of it. Crampon placements can be difficult because the bulge may block the climbers' line of sight with their feet. This series of movements is strenuous for the arms because it forces the climber to lean back away from the ice more than normal so as not to topple forward. (See figure 6-50.) 6-159. Traversing is challenging because it requires the climber to move deliberately out of balance and then back into balance with each move. The lead hand places a tool far to the side in the direction of travel. The climber then makes a short move in that direction. The rear tool is then moved into a new position closer to the centerline of the body. The climber then moves toward the lead tool again until it is close to the centerline of the body. The lead tool is then moved to a position further in the direction of travel and the sequence repeats. (See figure 6-50.) Another more advanced technique involves leap frogging the tools across the ice face to provide successive high tool placements. This requires changing hands on the high tool with each move and passing the rear tool to the lead hand before the next tool placement is made. Chapter 6 6-162. Climbing difficult mixed routes is impractical for military operations. However, easy to moderate mixed climbing (3rd- and 4th-class) is often necessary in alpine terrain. At the very least, transitioning back and forth between climbing low angle ice and snow and scrambling on rock in a cold environment is often necessary. TRAINING FOR ICE CLIMBING 6-163. Beginner ice climbing training is typically conducted at established climbing areas using top rope belay techniques (see chapter 10, section III). When supervised by qualified mountaineers, this kind of ice climbing is typically moderate risk and high payoff for developing mobility skill for small numbers of participants, if sufficient time is allotted. Top rope ice climbing sites are typically small or spread out. Training large groups effectively is difficult without special manufactured ice-climbing facilities. This is primarily due to the cold-weather environment in which ice develops. Ice climbing training should be planned along with concurrent training for smaller groups to rotate through. Route difficulty should be challenging for climbers, but easy enough that they can be successful. This motivates climbers to improve their skills. Chapter 7 Navigation in Mountainous Terrain The goals, strategies, and tools available to Soldiers for navigation in mountainous terrain are no different from other types of terrain. However, mountainous terrain makes using those tools to stay on course much more difficult. Additionally, straying off course while navigating in this terrain can prove extremely hazardous and detrimental to mission success. The difficulty of planning routes and calculating movement timelines also increases significantly with the steepness and complexity of terrain. Soldiers and leaders who learn how to mitigate these challenges effectively can not only successfully navigate in mountainous terrain but also better use the terrain for cover and concealment. SECTION I - MILITARY LAND NAVIGATION IN NONTECHNICAL MOUNTAINOUS TERRAIN 7-1. Navigation is the process of determining one's present position, locating a target objective, and selecting and following a route between these two points. Navigation consists of three distinct stages: orientation, navigation, and route finding. 7-2. Orientation is simply figuring out exactly where one is. Using a map, compass, and identifiable terrain features, assisted by an altimeter and GPS, is the foundation of good orientation. 7-3. Navigation determines the objective's location and the direction from the Soldier's starting point to the objective. The

one is. Using a map, compass, and identifiable terrain features, assisted by an altimeter and GPS, is the foundation of good orientation. 7-3. Navigation determines the objective's location and the direction from the Soldier's starting point to the objective. The same skills and equipment used in orientation are essential for good navigation. 7-4. Route finding is picking the best line of travel IAW METT-TC (I); mission, enemy, terrain and weather, troops and support available, time available, civil considerations, and informational considerations, and the commander's intent. Good route finding in mountainous terrain requires solid terrain analysis, clear priorities for route selection, an understanding of group members' levels of fitness and mobility skill, unit capabilities for technical movement, and mission-specific requirements. Examples of priorities for route selection are navigability of terrain, tactical advantage and disadvantage throughout the movement, concealment throughout, fatigue reduction, and required speed of movement. 7-5. Perhaps the single, most important factor in navigation through mountainous terrain is the ability to identify and analyze terrain. Navigators must be able to create an accurate mental model of the terrain to be moved through from a map or satellite imagery. The more skilled they are at this, the more effective they will

The more skilled they are at this, the more effective they will be at avoiding hazards, selecting tactically advantageous or concealed routes, and planning paths that minimize fatigue. This ability can only be developed effectively through route planning and movement in such terrain. Altimeters are valuable pieces of navigational equipment used by experienced navigators in mountainous terrain. They are rarely used in flatter terrain types. This information turns contour lines on a map into reliable linear features that can be followed, used as progress markers during movement, or as known points when they intersect with other clearly identifiable linear terrain features. 7-12. Most mountaineers use digital watch altimeters. 7-13. Altimeters use a barometer incorporated into their design to measure the weight of air above the device. Changes in the weather are usually accompanied by air pressure changes, which are reflected in the altimeter. As the air pressure drops due to the approach of inclement weather, for instance, the displayed elevation rises by a corresponding amount. Chapter 8 Knot Tying and Rope Management The rope is a vital piece of equipment to the mountaineer. It is used to address many of the problems and hazards encountered in the mountains. When climbing, rappelling, or building rope installations, the mountaineer must know how to utilize and maintain this equipment. Misuse can cause serious injury or death. This chapter discusses equipment, terminology, knots, hitches, rope management techniques, care, and maintenance. SECTION I - TYPES OF ROPE, WEBBING, AND CARABINERS 8-1. Mountaineering equipment is engineered to be lightweight but strong enough to provide a wide margin of safety. Each item is tested to high standards. In most cases, user error is to blame when this equipment fails. Soldiers should regularly check and inspect mountaineering equipment. Equipment should be replaced when there is any obvious damage, or it has exceeded the manufacturer's lifecycle recommendation. 8-2. All mountaineering equipment used in training should be constructed and tested to a recognized standard. The International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation, or Union des International Alpine Association (UIAA), is the certifying body that defines the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment. This safety commission develops the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment recognized throughout the world.

A static rope is a kernmantle rope designed for minimal stretch under load, primarily used for hauling, lowering, and anchor systems construction. A knot is the fixed portion of a rope that has been manipulated around itself, another object, or both during the process of being tied for some purpose. Knots are self-contained and self-supporting and do not need another object or rope to maintain its integrity. Hitches are not considered knots. Chapter 9 Anchor Selection and Construction Understanding anchors is an important fundamental that must be understood early in the path to becoming a military mountaineer. An anchor is the point where manufactured equipment for mountaineering meets the surface of the earth. Great varieties of natural features are found in different operational environments that a Soldier could use to construct an anchor. Anchors are found in all rope systems and are built in many ways. This chapter gives Soldiers the tools to assess terrain for the suitability of anchor construction for a wide variety of rope systems. This chapter also exposes Soldiers to the principles of anchor construction that ensure they are building solid anchors in a wide variety of terrain for many different purposes. Anchor selection in mountainous terrain requires a certain degree of knowledge and substantial experience. Most mountaineering accidents occur at the anchor. Inexperienced Soldiers should stick to selecting anchor features that are obviously stronger than necessary and choose simple rigging techniques with which they are familiar. SECTION I - GENERAL PRINCIPLES: SINGLE AND MULTIPOINT 9-1. An anchor for military mountaineering is a fixed object to which a rope system is secured and is of sufficient size, weight,

choose simple rigging techniques with which they are familiar. SECTION I - GENERAL PRINCIPLES: SINGLE AND MULTIPOINT 9-1. An anchor for military mountaineering is a fixed object to which a rope system is secured and is of sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load. It is a point in the operational environment, which a rope installation is attached, providing more than enough resistance to a directional pull. Rope systems can be used for moving casualties and equipment. Some, like rappels or fixed ropes, are used for aiding movement. Technical rope systems provide the tools for addressing many of the challenges posed by mountainous terrain. Anchor selection and evaluation together form the foundation of all systems. 9-2. Considerations for selecting a natural feature to construct an anchor are its location and ability to resist any forces that are placed upon it. The anchor should be above any intended rope pathways. This reduces the pendulum effect on any loads attached to the anchor. Another important facet of anchor location is its proximity to the edge. In some situations, having the anchor a short distance away from the edge creates a platform

This reduces the pendulum effect on any loads attached to the anchor. Another important facet of anchor location is its proximity to the edge. In some situations, having the anchor a short distance away from the edge creates a platform to work on. In other situations, such as setting a top rope, it is best to have the anchor near the edge. This aspect of anchor building can be challenging as the strength of natural features, such as rocks, trees, roots, and boulders; can be difficult to judge. Soldiers must err on the side of caution and leave no doubt that an anchor is strong enough for its intended purpose. If there is any doubt about a single-point anchor's strength or security, then additional anchor components should be constructed and incorporated until sufficient strength and security are achieved to ensure that anchor failure cannot occur. The strength of an anchor should never be in question. 9-3. Anchors in mountaineering should be loaded in a steady and slow manner. Avoid bouncing as much as possible as it could weaken the integrity of the natural object being used. Sometimes slack can generate in various types of rope systems and cause an anchor

be loaded in a steady and slow manner. Avoid bouncing as much as possible as it could weaken the integrity of the natural object being used. Sometimes slack can generate in various types of rope systems and cause an anchor to be shock loaded. It is best to avoid any circumstances that may lead to this as shock loading results in very high forces on the anchor. SINGLE-POINT ANCHORS 9-4. Single-point anchors are the simplest in mountaineering and serve as the building blocks for more complicated anchors. If a single feature, object, or piece of equipment is to be used as an anchor, there must be no doubt that it is both strong enough and secure enough to hold if shock loading were to occur. The same goes for all rigging used in building the anchor. Correctly tied master points, locking carabiners, and double nonlocking carabiners opposite and opposed must be used for all points of connection. Chapter 9 SECTION II - TREES 9-18. Tree anchors should be considered for use first. They are usually strong and often simple to construct with minimal use of equipment. Trees are already in place and simply require a method of attaching the rope. However, they should be carefully studied and evaluated for stability and strength before use. Sometimes the rope is tied directly to the anchor, but under most circumstances, a cord or sling is attached to the tree and then the climbing rope is attached to the sling with a carabiner. rope should be anchored as low as possible to reduce leverage. * When evaluating a tree for suitable strength, strive for a diameter at the base of the tree of at least 8 inches. * In the summer months, it may be easy to determine if a tree is alive. The best indicator can be leaves. However, even trees that have fallen over may still grow leaves if they are still partially rooted. Ensure that a concentrated effort is made to evaluate the tree. * In the winter, certain trees do not have leaves. This may make it difficult to establish if they are alive. A high-strength tie off is a single-point anchoring method that retains maximum installation rope strength and releasability, using multiple-round turns around the anchor object to create friction, and securing the end back to itself ensuring no force is applied to any component knots or carabiners. It is used to anchor the rope on high-load installations used for bridging and traversing. (See figure 9-9, page 206.) The wraps of the rope around the anchor absorb the tension of the installation and keep the tension off the knot and carabiner. The anchor is usually tied with a minimum of three wraps, more, if necessary, to absorb the tension. A smooth anchor may require several wraps, whereas a rough barked tree might only require a few. The rope is wrapped from top to bottom without crossing strands so that it can be untied under tension, if desired. A fixed loop is placed into the end of the rope and attached loosely back onto the rope with a locking carabiner. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 205

Chapter 9 Figure 9-11. Chockstone used in a construction TUNNELS, ARCHES, AND PINCH POINTS 9-26. Tunnels and arches are holes formed in solid rock. If viable, they provide one of the more secure natural anchor points as they can be pulled in any direction (See figure 9-12.) A natural anchor is a natural fixed object (such as a tree, rock formation, or ice formation) to which a rope system can be secured and is of sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load. A sling is threaded through the opening hole and secured with a joining knot or girth hitch. The load-bearing hole must be strong and free of sharp edges (pad, if necessary). A pinch-point anchor is used the same way as arches or tunnels; it is just formed by a pinch point between two large boulders, allowing a sling or cordelette to be tied around it. Boulders comprising a pinch point need to be large enough and secure enough to ensure they do not move when a force is applied. Pitons still have a place in military mountaineering since they are a relatively light, cheap, and expendable yet extremely strong and secure anchor option when placed properly.
