Chapter 9 BOLTS 9-39. A bolt is a type of rock protection or anchoring component comprised of an expansion bolt or glue-in shaft attached to a hanger to which a carabiner can be attached. Bolts are often used in fixed-rope installations and in aid climbing where cracks are not available. Bolts provide one of the most secure means of establishing protection. 9-40. Some bolts have rings attached for easy retrievable rappelling, clip-in points for top rope climbing, chains to aid in establishing tope rope climbing anchors, or other special-purpose attachment points. 9-41. There are two primary types of bolts: expansion bolts and glue-in bolts. Both involve drilling a hole into a rock face, cleaning out dust and debris, and inserting a bolt. The difference is in how the bolt is secured in the hole: * Expansion bolts use a sleeve that expands as it is tightened. The sleeve expands against the walls of the hole to prevent it from coming out. (See figure 9-16.) * Glue-in bolts are held in place by a high-strength adhesive. Glue-in bolts are used in softer, porous rock, such as sandstone. Delicate rock, like sandstone, may not be strong enough to support expansion bolts. Its

Anchor Selection and Construction INSTALLATION AND USE 9-44. There are enough differences in bolts available on the market that mountaineers should refer to manufacturers' instructions for installing bolts. Installing bolts permanently alters the rock. The climbing community has strong ethics regarding the placement of bolts. Ethics and regulations vary regionally, but in all areas, it is unacceptable to add bolts to existing climbs. Any bolting should be done with the consensus of the climbing community. 9-45. When using existing bolts as climbing protection or as part of an anchor system, mountaineers should inspect them for anything indicating compromise. The first thing that should be inspected is the rock on which it will be placed. Bolts are only as strong and secure as the quality of the rock. The hanger should not be rusty or loose. Loose hangers can indicate the bolt being insecure, or the hole has not been drilled deep enough to secure the hanger to the rock's face. If the nut holding a hanger can be tightened to a point, then it is viable. If it keeps spinning, the bolt should not be used or at the very least backed up with additional protection. 9-46. Using chocks in anchor construction has the following advantages: * Tactically quiet installation and recovery. * Usually easy to retrieve and, unless severely damaged, are reusable. * Light to carry. * Minimal rock scarring as opposed to pitons. * Sometimes can be placed where pitons cannot (expanding rock flakes where pitons would further weaken the rock). 9-49. Using chock in anchor construction has the following disadvantages: * May not fit in thin cracks, which may accept pitons. * Often provide only one direction of pull. * Practice and experience are necessary to become proficient in proper placement and removal. PLACEMENT 9-50. The principles of placing chocks are to find a crack with a constriction at some point, place a chock of appropriate size above and behind the constriction, and set the chock by gently jerking down. Maximum surface contact with a tight fit is critical. Chocks are usually good for a single direction of pull. 9-51. Avoid cracks that have crumbly (soft) or deteriorating rock, if possible. Some cracks may have loose rock, grass, and dirt, which should be removed before placing the chock. Look for a constriction point in the

When selecting a chock, choose one that has as much surface area as possible in contact with the rock. A chock resting on one small crystal or point of rock is likely to be unsafe. A chock that sticks partly out of the crack is avoided. 9-53. Anchor Selection and Construction 9-54. Chocks must be lightly tugged on to set them so that they do not fall out of placement. Weighting the placement helps to keep the protection in position. A carabiner often provides enough weight. CAMMING DEVICES 9-55. Camming devices are designed for building anchors in parallel-sided cracks where chocks are ineffective. There are several different types, but they all work by changing from a downward force to an outward force when loaded. This force creates enough friction that the device cannot move, even when no constriction in the crack is present. Camming devices increase force on surrounding rock as downward force is applied. Due to this, care should be taken to inspect the security of the rock on which they are placed. 9-56. Camming devices become even more secure when placed above a constriction. If the lobes slip during loading, they cannot exit the crack. 9-57. Cams are the most used camming devices in mountaineering. They have advantages and disadvantages and require extensive practice and experience to place and use properly. SPRING-LOADED CAMMING DEVICES 9-58. Cams are the most versatile and widely used artificial rock anchoring devices available to mountaineers. Although there are several types

They have advantages and disadvantages and require extensive practice and experience to place and use properly. SPRING-LOADED CAMMING DEVICES 9-58. Cams are the most versatile and widely used artificial rock anchoring devices available to mountaineers. Although there are several types of cams, the modern design consists of two sets of lobes that oppose each other and rotate from one or two axles, connected to a trigger mechanism on a single, flexible stem that runs perpendicular to the axle. Attached to the axle is a presewn connection sling. They are designed to work in parallel-sided cracks where a chock would just slide down. 9-59. Cams come in a wide variety of sizes to fit cracks from 0.5 inches to over 21 inches. Each unit has an expansion range that enables it to function properly within a certain width of cracks. It may be necessary to carry many sizes depending upon the route, mission, and intended use. Most come with color-coded slings to help the user select the correct size for use. 9-60. Three quality camming devices equalized together are required to establish an adequate anchor. An exception is two large camming devices perfectly placed in solid rock with constrictions below them.

Suboptimal placements or rock features require additional pieces to achieve an acceptable anchor. ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES 9-61. The disadvantages of using cams in anchor construction are listed below: * They can wiggle or walk out of proper placement, resulting in a compromised anchor, or in a stuck camming device that is difficult or

Chapter 9 9-75. The security of an ice screw is determined by the quality of the ice in which it is placed. The thicker and denser the ice is, the stronger it is. Thinner ice, aerated ice, or ice with air pockets is weak; mountaineers should avoid this sort of ice. Deep, thick ice is generally bluish in color, while ice that has air pockets is often white in color. It takes significant experience to judge the strength of ice, but even a novice can learn much about ice quality by the resistance felt when placing the ice screw. Air pockets are felt as a reduction in resistance. The more resistance, the denser the ice. The longer the core grows as it is screwed in, typically the better the ice. (See figure 9-23.) Evaluate the integrity of the ice structure. If possible, avoid fracture lines, the apex of ice bulges, and ice blocks that are not attached to a main flow. Figure 9-23. The art of constructing and placing good earth anchors requires a great deal of practice and experience. It is especially important to load earth anchors in a slow and steady manner. A deadman is an effective means of building an anchor in earth or snow when there are no other natural anchors available. A deadman is constructed by digging a trench perpendicular to the direction of pull and placing a lengthy solid object with a sling or cordelette attached into it. Chapter 10 Rope Systems for Climbing There is an inherent risk to moving in the mountains. Much of the terrain is high consequence, where a misjudged foothold, a loose rock, a slip, trip, or fall can kill. However, troops fighting in the mountains are often exposed to greater risk by not being able to move through the terrain. Examples exist throughout history. Modern examples include the assaults on Riva Ridge and Monte la Difensa in Italy, both examples of failed conventional assaults, where defensive positions in the heights were taken by assaults through more difficult terrain. More recently, the Indians retaking hilltops in the Kargil Conflict display all the same principles. Successful offensive operations in the mountains require troops who can move in difficult terrain and under poor conditions. The alternative is costly, often unsuccessful attacks where the defenders hold significant tactical advantage. To manage the risk involved with movement through these types of terrain, Soldiers must be trained in a variety of rope systems for climbing. SECTION I - RISK MITIGATION 10-1. Fighting in the mountains requires exposure to mountain hazards. The mountain environment is defined by its hazards and difficulties. Often, the control measures used to address one

a variety of rope systems for climbing. SECTION I - RISK MITIGATION 10-1. Fighting in the mountains requires exposure to mountain hazards. The mountain environment is defined by its hazards and difficulties. Often, the control measures used to address one hazard increase the exposure to another. Installing or using ropes to protect against a fall increases movement time and increases the exposure to compromise by enemy forces. MANAGING RISK 10-2. Managing risk in the mountains is a dynamic process, where the most appropriate measures for managing risk change with the terrain and situation. 10-3. Control measures target either the consequence or the likelihood of an incident. Protective equipment, such as a helmet to protect against rockfall, only reduces the consequence. The likelihood of being hit by rockfall is addressed by avoiding areas of loose rock and routing Soldiers so that they do not travel above one another. REDUCING THE LIKELIHOOD OF A FALL 10-4. The mountaineer has several technical tools for managing fall hazards. However, while the consequence of a fall can be reduced, it cannot be eliminated. Even a short fall while rock climbing can cause severe injury. To manage the risk, target factors that will reduce the likelihood

for managing fall hazards. However, while the consequence of a fall can be reduced, it cannot be eliminated. Even a short fall while rock climbing can cause severe injury. To manage the risk, target factors that will reduce the likelihood of a fall. JUDGEMENT 10-5. The safety of a mountaineer comes from the ability to read the terrain. Judge the rock, snow, or ice, and see where it can be climbed and where it cannot. This includes identifying features and weaknesses that can be linked together. Judgement is developed through time spent climbing in a controlled environment and through experience and mentorship. TECHNIQUE 10-6. Soldiers must possess the physical ability to make the moves, use footholds, and maintain balance as each move is made. As with judgement, climbing technique is the product of extensive training. LOAD 10-7. Increased Soldier load rapidly increases the difficulty of climbing, even in easy terrain. Operations in the mountains are subject to the mindset that occupying high terrain requires more equipment for sustaining life than at lower elevations. However, to maintain maneuverability, the Soldier's load must be reduced. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 235

Chapter 10 Soldiers conducting offensive operations, reconnaissance patrols, or any maneuver in high-consequence terrain need to travel light. FOOTWEAR 10-8. Proper footwear will enhance the military mountaineer's ability to move safely and efficiently through the rugged terrain found in the mountains. (See chapter 4 for footwear considerations.) ROPE 10-9. Ropes are used to reduce the consequence of a fall. Ropes can be fixed in place to manage or reduce the consequences of a fall (see chapter 11) or can be used to provide belays (see section III in this chapter). SECTION II - CONSIDERATIONS FOR MOVING UNROPED 10-10. Moving unroped is the fastest and most efficient method of moving through terrain. It requires little equipment and is quiet. Team members can move together, making communication quiet and easy. In instances where the greatest hazard is not falling, but rock or icefall, impending severe weather threat, enemy observation, or failing to meet an operational timeline, moving unroped may be the safest way to move. (See figure 10-1.) Moving unroped in terrain above 3rd-class should only be done after thorough risk analysis has been conducted and speed has been identified as a critical control measure for managing overall operational risk. SECTION III - BELAYED CLIMBING 10-13. A belay is a system of using a rope as a backup in steep terrain to arrest a Soldier's fall should one occur. This section will discuss an overview of various strategies for using ropes and belays. TYPES OF BELAYED CLIMBING 10-14. When terrain is too dangerous to move unroped, a team will transition to belayed climbing. Belayed climbing is usually done in a party of two, with each climber tied into one end of the rope. One team member is always anchored and providing a belay for the other. TOP ROPE CLIMBING 10-15. Military mountaineers are first introduced to top rope climbing. Top rope climbing is where the rope is run through

end of the rope. One team member is always anchored and providing a belay for the other. TOP ROPE CLIMBING 10-15. Military mountaineers are first introduced to top rope climbing. Top rope climbing is where the rope is run through an anchor at the top of a climb and kept relatively snug to avoid longer falls. It is a training tool used to teach climbing technique. (See section IV for more information on top rope climbing.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 237

Chapter 10 LEAD CLIMBING 10-16. As military mountaineers progress, they are later introduced to lead climbing. Lead climbing is climbing a route while attached to the end of a rope to place devices in rock, ice, or snow for fall protection with a belayer located below. When lead climbing, one climber leads climbs, placing protection and clipping the rope through it as they go. The belayer (sometimes referred to as the second) belays and is prepared to catch a fall. Lead climbers climb to another secure stance, build a solid anchor, and then belay second climbers as they climb to the new stance. Each length of climbing is called a pitch, which is a section of a climb that comprises the distance between two belay stations, which can be up to a standard rope length (60 meters) on easy ice and snow. In more broken rock, it may be just 10 to 15 meters, to minimize rope drag and aid communication. 10-17. Lead climbing provides security for both members of the party. Leaders accept more risk because they are climbing above their protection. Any fall will be well past the last piece of protection they placed before the rope begins

communication. 10-17. Lead climbing provides security for both members of the party. Leaders accept more risk because they are climbing above their protection. Any fall will be well past the last piece of protection they placed before the rope begins to come tight, so it is still imperative that leaders have good movement skills. The second has a top rope unless the route traverses. The overall security of the team is good. The team always has a solid attachment, and the belays can be placed in sheltered stances, with solid anchors. (See section V for more information on lead climbing.) 10-18. Most climbers will protect themselves with belays in 5th-class terrain. In 3rd- or 4th-class terrain, in darkness or bad weather, belayed climbing is the most conservative strategy for protecting the team and provides the greatest margin of safety. AID CLIMBING 10-19. If the climbing is too difficult for the leader, aid climbing is a climbing technique in which standing on or pulling oneself up via devices attached to fixed or placed protection is used to make upward progress. (See figure 10-2.) Aid climbing is when climbers use anchors and protection to support their weight as they climb. In a

Simul-climbing is a belay technique involving two Soldiers climbing simultaneously while attached to the ends of a rope which runs through the fall protection. It is a variation of belayed climbing, where leaders continue to climb rather than stopping to belay the second. Second climbers climb simultaneously, removing protection as they go. Leaders continue to climb while trying to keep a few pieces of protection between the two climbers at all times. If one falls, they may pull their teammate off their stance, but they will be caught eventually, counterbalanced through the protection with the other climber. Simul-climbing is faster than belayed climbing and useful for covering easy ground quickly. (See figure 10-3, page 240.) Simul-climbing provides more security than soloing. Climbers may find it necessary to shorten ropes between 20 and 30 meters to help with communication and prevent rope drag. 10-22. When both climbers are moving together, both share the consequence of a fall. Climbers should only use simul-climbing where a fall is unlikely and with partners of similar ability. Rope Systems for Climbing Short Roping 10-24. Short roping is a technique that may have some use in training military mountaineers. (See figure 10-4, page 242.) Short roping is used by more experienced mountaineers for protecting less experienced Soldiers in easy but exposed terrain. The climbing rope is shortened to just a few meters, and the leader holds the rope close to the other's harness and the two move together. Short roping cannot arrest a fall. It manages risk by putting the senior mountaineer close to the other climber, where the senior mountaineer can coach and model. If someone slips, leaders pull the rope connected to their harness to prevent the slip from becoming a fall. The only anchor is the senior mountaineer's stance. Short roping is appropriate only in terrain where leaders are confident climbing unroped and do not need their hands to climb. 10-25. Short roping has limited application for military mountaineers. Short roping requires practice and the leader's full attention. In an operational environment, the military mountaineer's focus must be forward, looking for upcoming hazards or enemy contact. Chapter 10 Figure 10-6. Kiwi coil OPERATIONAL CONSIDERATIONS 10-32. The various strategies and techniques described above for moving while roped will compromise speed and security. In a training environment, safety and conservative decision making must be the primary focus. As military mountaineers progress in their training, they may be exposed to alpine terrain above tree line. Weather and environmental hazards can pose a greater threat than falling. Each strategy for protecting the movement of the team is a compromise that should match the difficulty of terrain and the consequence of a fall. It should not expose the team to greater risk from another hazard. For combat operations, military mountaineers may need to compromise on protection and belays even further. Speed, stealth, and the ability to react are critical if enemy contact is expected. SECTION IV - TOP ROPE CLIMBING 10-33. A top rope is a belay in which both rope ends are on the ground and the rope runs up to the top of the cliff (or climb) and passes through a pre-established anchor point. This enables one Soldier to climb while the other Soldier belays. The belayer keeps the rope tight to prevent the climber from falling more than

to the top of the cliff (or climb) and passes through a pre-established anchor point. This enables one Soldier to climb while the other Soldier belays. The belayer keeps the rope tight to prevent the climber from falling more than a short distance. This system also enables the belayer to lower the climber back down to the ground after completing the climb. (See figure 10-7 for an example of top rope climbing.) 244 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

It allows Soldiers to learn the fundamentals of tying in and belaying and to practice individual climbing techniques without the consequences of a long leader fall or unroped fall. It allows one instructor to coach and supervise both the climber and the belayer. It also facilitates learning the climbing technique because all participants can observe one another. EQUIPMENT CONSIDERATIONS 10-35. The UIAA develops safety and testing standards for mountaineering equipment. Equipment used for any mountaineering training should meet these standards as outlined in chapter 8 and appendix C. HELMETS 10-36. Helmets will protect a Soldier from rockfall and debris. They also offer some protection from impacts in a swinging fall. Climbing helmets are lightweight and certified to standards set by the UIAA. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 245

Chapter 10 10-37. Most units do not have access to climbing helmets. The combat helmet, while not rated or designed for impact protection from rockfall or in climbing falls, is already issued to most Soldiers and provides adequate protection. HARNESS 10-38. There are many types of climbing harnesses. Harnesses must be made and tested to UIAA standards, and users must ensure that wear and use conforms to manufacturer recommendations. The high-angle mountaineering kit (HAMK) is issued to units where most Soldiers have no formal mountaineering training. The harness that was selected for the HAMK (see figure 10-8), is a harness with a single, reinforced tie-in portion. It is a simpler harness than most recreational climbing harnesses. It is one-size fits all and easy to put on and inspect. It has one gear loop on the left side, which can be used to rack equipment. When worn, it should be tight around the waist, with the leg loops snug enough to take some of the force while falling or sitting into the harness. 10-39. take some of the force while falling or sitting into the harness. 10-39. If harnesses are not available, tubular webbing can be used to make field expedient harnesses, although this is not preferred. Dynamic ropes stretch and reduce the peak impact force felt by a climber in a fall. Falls while top roping should not generate as much force as a lead fall; however, if slack develops in the belay, such as from a stuck rope or slow belayer, there is potential for generating significant force. 10-42. Heavy-duty climbing ropes in the 10-mm range are recommended for top rope training. The 10.2-mm dynamic rope included in the ACTKs provides good durability. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 247

Chapter 10 PREPARATION 10-43. Advanced and master military mountaineers should plan and supervise mountaineering training that involves roped climbing and rappelling. They advise the commander on training requirements, priorities, and equipment needs, as well as plan, organize, and conduct training. SITE RECONNAISSANCE 10-44. Visit the training area before the scheduled training date and conduct a rehearsal or walkthrough with key personnel. This will help proof the plan, identify hazards, and develop controls. It is also an opportunity to save time with set up by identifying anchors and cleaning the area of loose rock or other hazards ahead of time. TIME MANAGEMENT 10-45. Ensure the training plan provides ample time to cover movement, set up, demonstrations, and training time. Extra time for contingencies is often needed. COMMUNICATION 10-46. All key personnel should have reliable communication with each other to communicate changes to hazards or conditions or to coordinate the response to emergencies. The procedures for conducting a lead climb with a group of two are relatively simple. The most experienced individual is the lead climber or leader. Leaders are responsible for selecting the route. No matter how direct the route, the climber often encounters problems with rope drag through the protection positions. Rope drag is caused when there are exaggerated changes in direction of the rope between carabiners attached to protection that creates excessive friction. Minimal rope drag is an inconvenience; severe rope drag may pull the climber off balance, inducing a fall. When belaying the second, rope drag can be mistaken for the climber, causing the belayer to not take in the necessary slack. This can potentially result in a serious fall. To prevent this, the placements should be extended by using runners, when necessary, so the rope creates a smooth, almost straight line as it passes through the carabiners. (See figure 10-16.) Do this by attaching an appropriate-length runner to the protection to extend the rope connection in the necessary direction. The runner is attached to the protection while the rope is clipped into a carabiner at the opposite end of the runner. Chapter 10 SECTION VI - ALPINE BELAY TECHNIQUES 10-118. In broken alpine terrain, with secure stances, and no chance of second climbers falling and hanging from a belay, hasty techniques may provide adequate protection for the team. Safety should never be compromised for the sake of speed. Use of standard belay techniques should be used if there is any question as to security. BODY BELAYS 10-119. Body belays can sometimes be used on short sections of less steep terrain where a fall is unlikely and there is a good, braced belay stance of which to take advantage. To create a body belay, simply run the rope around the body at the waist to create friction, with the chest facing the direction of pull. The load rope is at one hip and the brake strand is in the opposite side hand. To take in rope, pull in on the load rope with the guide hand and out with the brake hand. Grab both ropes above the brake hand with the guide hand and slide the brake hand back towards the body. To brake, pull the brake hand up and across the chest. The body belay can be used in either the

Grab both ropes above the brake hand with the guide hand and slide the brake hand back towards the body. To brake, pull the brake hand up and across the chest. The body belay can be used in either the sitting or standing position; however, the sitting position offers a lower center of gravity and is preferred. It can also be used with an anchor or without. The advantage of the body belay is its speed and simplicity for belaying short sections where a climber is moving quickly. However, there are disadvantages as well. Because the force of a fall is dissipated as friction against belayers' bodies, serious rope burns can occur to the body and hands, possibly causing them to lose control of the belay. It also generates less braking force and causes more slippage than other techniques, causing the climber to fall farther. For this reason, it is only used on low-angle easy terrain. The belayer must have a good, braced position and must keep the rope tight. (See figure 10-21.) 268 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

The shoulder belay shares many of the advantages and disadvantages listed above for the body belay. The level of friction created with this method is relatively low and should only be used on short steps where there is no risk of the climber hanging from the belay in a fall. A classic example of terrain where the shoulder belay is appropriate is a short, steep step where the belayer can stand directly above the climber below. The rope is routed under the arm, over the opposite shoulder, and down to the opposite hand and is kept tight with the climber below. The belayer's body creates friction on the rope and acts as the anchor at the same time. A shoulder belay is fast to create, but it is only suitable on rare occasions. (See figure 10-22, page 270.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 269

Chapter 11 Fixed Ropes Fixed ropes are an important part of military mountaineering as they facilitate the movement of Soldiers through rugged terrain. Fixed ropes allow large groups of Soldiers to safely access terrain that provides tactical advantage over the enemy. They have proven useful in past conflicts. During World War II, they were successfully used during Operation Neptune (commonly referred to as D-day) and the famous assault on Riva Ridge by the 10th Mountain Division. Proficiency in using fixed ropes allows units to overcome mobility limitations and, therefore, achieve greater lethality in mountainous terrain. SECTION I - BASIC FIXED-ROPE TECHNIQUES 11-1. A fixed rope is any rope system attached to at least one anchor that can be used to improve security and efficiency of movement through difficult terrain that subjects Soldiers to a fall hazard. They can be used for ascending, descending, or traversing across steep terrain in which a fall hazard exists. They may simply provide Soldiers with a handhold through a short section of steep terrain or as complex as hundreds of feet of broken hazardous terrain involving numerous sections that prevent attached Soldiers from being able to fall. They can be used to assist the movement

a handhold through a short section of steep terrain or as complex as hundreds of feet of broken hazardous terrain involving numerous sections that prevent attached Soldiers from being able to fall. They can be used to assist the movement of small teams to large units. They allow units to overcome mobility limitations and access tactically advantageous terrain. FIXED-ROPE CONSIDERATIONS 11-2. Fixed ropes should be used whenever a group of Soldiers cannot move safely through a section of terrain unroped. Fixed ropes are usually the most efficient means of protecting groups larger than team sized, especially if the groups have not received advanced military mountaineering training. Common factors contributing to the necessity of building fixed ropes are fall hazard, slippery surfaces, limited visibility, heavy loads, low mobility skills, and fatigue. 11-3. The two basic types of fixed-rope systems are simple fixed ropes and fixed ropes with intermediate anchors. Both types have applications in every class of terrain. Simple fixed ropes are anchored only at the top, can only be used by one Soldier at a time, and require a straight path of movement from bottom to top. Fixed ropes with intermediate anchors have multiple anchors and rope sections, allowing more

are anchored only at the top, can only be used by one Soldier at a time, and require a straight path of movement from bottom to top. Fixed ropes with intermediate anchors have multiple anchors and rope sections, allowing more Soldiers to move on them simultaneously and the path to change directions. Each type is determined by route and availability of anchors along it, the number of Soldiers to use the system, and the type of available equipment to attach to it. 11-4. All types of fixed ropes are built from the top down over, or through, terrain obstacles. However, fixed rope installation teams may need to ascend terrain using other techniques prior to building a fixed-rope system. (See chapter 10.) 11-5. Units planning to use fixed ropes must establish installation teams capable of locating routes, moving safely through various terrain obstacles, and building a variety of installations. They should be led by advanced military mountaineers but may be assisted by basic military mountaineers. These teams should be experienced in building fixed ropes in the type of terrain to be negotiated, equipped appropriately for the task, and familiar with the capabilities of the Soldiers who use them. 11-6. In a tactical environment, any terrain that requires a fixed rope should be considered a VDA, which is steep terrain that puts a unit moving through it at significant tactical disadvantage. The process for establishing even the simplest fixed rope comes at the cost of time and exposure to enemy attack. Adequate security must be established prior to deploying the installation team. In complex terrain, security teams may need to be adjusted or leap-frogged forward if fixed-rope systems cover large pieces of terrain. a handhold for balance, sliding the prusik up to capture progress and prevent fall in case of a slip. 11-14. The characteristics of the Soldiers who use the fixed rope are also useful information. Particularly, what their mobility and technical skill levels are and what equipment they have for attaching to the rope. 278 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Intermediate Anchors 11-24. Terrain and vegetation determine the equipment mountaineers need to build the fixed rope. Heavily vegetated terrain or broken rocky terrain may only require cordelettes, slings, and carabiners. Slabby or steep rock faces require cams, nuts, and other lead climbing protection to build anchors. Intermediate anchors must be built robust enough to support the weight of a fall by the number of Soldiers who will move on each section at a given time. When possible, anchors should be built at about waist height in places where good footing is possible so that transitioning past anchors is easier for Soldiers moving on the fixed rope (See figure 11-3 for common methods of attaching ropes to single component anchors.) Rope Section Slack 11-25. Fixed-rope sections do not have a standard amount of slack. There should be enough slack to allow Soldiers to follow the easiest path through terrain without adding fall risk. Sometimes a lot of slack is necessary to go around an obstacle or steep section. This is usually better than running a tighter rope over these things, because going around is easier, which reduces the chance of a fall. Other times, a section may need to

Other times, a section may need to be tight to reduce fall distance, such as traversing across a cliff on a narrow ledge. Figure 11-3. Intermediate anchors in moderate terrain, example ATTACHMENT AND MOVEMENT 11-26. The method for movement on fixed ropes with intermediate anchors is as important as how they are constructed. Two primary methods exist for use in steep terrain: the two personal safeties method and the ascender-carabiner method. Choosing between the two is a tradeoff between not carrying heavier single-purpose items and having more security during movement. The two personal safeties method requires no special equipment but cannot eliminate fall risk for a Soldier. The ascender-carabiner method prevents falling but requires each Soldier to carry a piece of equipment that has little other use. Both techniques have their place, and both must be considered for use when planning fixed-rope movements. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 279

Chapter 11 Two Personal Safeties Method 11-27. This method involves having two separate girth hitched slings attached to the tie-in portion of the harness with a single nonlocking carabiner in each. The carabiners are then attached to the fixed rope. Always keep the two carabiners attached to the rope unless they move past an intermediate anchor. To move past an intermediate anchor, clip one carabiner at a time above the anchor. When both carabiners are above the anchor, continue movement. (See figure 11-4.) 11-28. The two personal safeties method is appropriate for situations where the fall consequence is high, but the likelihood is low. It can be used up to 4th-class terrain under good conditions (such as good surface conditions, moderate mobility skills, light loads, well-rested, high visibility) provided that intermediate anchors are appropriately spaced to prevent serious fall injury. Since falls using this method are only stopped by the last anchor a Soldier passed, there is always a chance of injury. This should be considered carefully before choosing it. Figure 11-4. Two personal safeties attachment 280 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Ascender-Carabiner Method 11-29. The ascender-carabiner method is the fastest and most secure way to travel up very steep fixed ropes. It is preferred when fall risk is substantial or sections of the fixed rope are long, because the ascender captures the Soldiers' progress as they move. 11-30. To use this technique, girth hitch two slings into the harness. Clip one nonlocking carabiner into one extension. Clip a mechanical ascender to the other extension with a locking carabiner. 11-31. Ascend in the same manner as with simple fixed ropes. To move past the intermediate anchor, clip the nonlocking carabiner above the anchor, and then move the ascender to above the carabiner on the fixed rope. (See figure 11-5.) 11-32. This method is appropriate when both fall consequence and likelihood are high. It can be used in terrain up to 4th class under any conditions. It is the best method when surface conditions are slippery, loads are heavy, mobility skills are low or Soldiers are fatigued, during low visibility, and when intermediate anchors cannot be established to prevent fall injury. Figure 11-5. Ascender-carabiner method 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 281

Chapter 11 FIXED ROPES IN VERTICAL TERRAIN 11-33. Fixed ropes are sometimes necessary for moving in vertical terrain during complex rescue operations or other special operations in permissive or nontactical environments. They are rarely practical for tactical operations, given their extreme exposure to enemy observation and direct fire. However, vertical terrain is not always avoidable during combat operations, and there are historical examples of their use during pivotal cliff assaults. Vertical terrain is the most extreme example of VDA. Soldiers moving on vertically fixed ropes require well-established overwatch security since they are totally exposed and can do little but ascend the fixed rope. 11-34. Moving on fixed ropes in vertical terrain requires Soldiers to possess the equipment and skills necessary to ascend rope, relying entirely on their attachment to it to prevent fall. Efficient ascending requires specialized equipment. CONSTRUCTING FIXED ROPES IN VERTICAL TERRAIN 11-35. Fixed ropes in vertical terrain are constructed in the same fashion as moderate terrain; however, they take greater technical rope skills, experience with complex anchoring, and time to establish. With fixed ropes in moderate terrain, it would be ideal for the installation team to approach the route from the top and build the system top-down.

they take greater technical rope skills, experience with complex anchoring, and time to establish. With fixed ropes in moderate terrain, it would be ideal for the installation team to approach the route from the top and build the system top-down. However, this is rarely possible. Typically, they must be established from the bottom up by advanced military mountaineers employing lead climbing techniques to get the rope to the top. This process is time-consuming and inherently risky. ASCENDING TECHNIQUES 11-36. Many situations may require a Soldier to ascend a rope in very steep or vertical terrain. Soldiers must be prepared and equipped to do so when operating in 4th- and 5th-class terrain. Typically, ascending rope is a more efficient technique than climbing for moving followers over hard climbing terrain, to include those members of small assault climber teams. 11-37. The techniques described below are for single strands of rope, so it is imperative that appropriate measures are taken to pad the rope near sharp edges. Whenever Soldiers plan to ascend vertical terrain, they should use mechanical ascenders to achieve maximum safety and efficiency during movement. 11-38. Ascending techniques are also key skills used in rescue operations, self-rescue during crevasse fall, and

rope near sharp edges. Whenever Soldiers plan to ascend vertical terrain, they should use mechanical ascenders to achieve maximum safety and efficiency during movement. 11-38. Ascending techniques are also key skills used in rescue operations, self-rescue during crevasse fall, and whenever rappellers find their rope does not reach the ground. Prusik Ascent 11-39. Two prusiks can be used to ascend rope. One prusik is tied to the fixed rope using a cordelette at approximately forehead height. A fixed loop is tied in the hanging tails to create an attachment point at about waist level. This is then secured to the harness with a locking carabiner. Another prusik is tied to the fixed rope at about waist level. The hanging tails are then tied to one or both feet using any appropriate knot to form a foot stirrup. (See figure 11-6.) 11-40. The upper prusik serves as the "progress capture," during ascent, by holding the Soldier up, while the lower friction hitch serves as the "progress" or makeshift foothold. During movement, the lower hitch is slid up as high as possible while hanging from the upper hitch. Soldiers then stand up on the lower hitch, pushing down and behind them with

hitch serves as the "progress" or makeshift foothold. During movement, the lower hitch is slid up as high as possible while hanging from the upper hitch. Soldiers then stand up on the lower hitch, pushing down and behind them with their leg, while sliding the upper hitch as high as possible. They then rest in the harness from the upper hitch and continue. Safety knots should be tied in the fixed rope below the lower hitch and attached to the harness with a locking carabiner every 10 to 15 feet. This provides a backup against failure of the friction hitch to grab. This technique should be considered an improvised technique for use when ascending is not expected. 282 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Figure 11-6. Prusik ascent Prusik Ascender Method 11-41. Mechanical ascenders are a one-directional device used to capture progress along a rope and assist climbers as they ascend steep, vertical, or free-hanging terrain. They can be substituted for one or both hitches described in prusik ascent. They make ascending efficient and fast. 11-42. To use an ascender as a progress capture, attach it to the rope at about head height. Girth hitch a sling or cordelette to the harness, and then use a locking carabiner to secure the other end to the bottom of the ascender, forming an arm-length extension between them. Commonly, a nonlocking carabiner is clipped around the rope through the top of the ascender for added security. This prevents the device from twisting off the rope. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 283

Chapter 11 11-43. To create the progress with an ascender, attach it to the rope at about waist height. Girth hitch or use any carabiner to attach a sling or cordelette to the bottom of the carabiner and tie it to one or both feet using any appropriate knot. The movement process is the same as described above for prusik ascent. 11-44. There are dozens of devices available that work the same as an ascender. Ensure the rope type and diameter are appropriate for the device used, as most mechanical devices have a specified range of acceptable use. Read all manufacturers' instructions to ensure safe use. 11-45. Stopper knots should be tied in the fixed rope below the lower hitch or device and attached to the harness with a locking carabiner every 10 to 15 feet. This provides a backup against the rope grabs slipping. This technique should be used when ascending is planned but not enough ascenders are available for Soldiers to be issued two. Double-Ascender Method 11-46. This technique is extremely efficient once it has been practiced. It is a recommended technique for ascending long distances. An etrier or cordelette forming a foot stirrup is hung off each

for Soldiers to be issued two. Double-Ascender Method 11-46. This technique is extremely efficient once it has been practiced. It is a recommended technique for ascending long distances. An etrier or cordelette forming a foot stirrup is hung off each ascender with a locking carabiner. Both ascenders are then placed on the rope. A cordelette or sling also hangs off each ascender and is girth hitched to the user's harness, creating two attachment points to the rope. (See figure 11-7.) 11-47. To use the system, the Soldier places a foot in each etrier (or stirrup) and slides the upper ascender up the rope. This upper ascender is easier to move because the Soldier's weight is on the lower ascender. The lower ascender is moved up next, while the upper ascender supports the Soldier's weight. Sometimes it is necessary to slightly release the camming mechanism before moving an ascender. 11-48. It is also recommended to tie back-up knots periodically in the same manner as prusik ascent. 11-49. This technique is the most efficient and is recommended for use whenever ascending is a planned movement technique. 284 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Figure 11-7. Double-ascender ascent SPECIAL TECHNIQUES AND CONSIDERATIONS 11-50. There are too many considerations for using and improving fixed ropes to cover them all in this training circular. However, the following techniques should be considered for use with fixed ropes. Weapon Management 11-51. Unless enemy attack is imminent, weapons should be slung to the rear, allowing Soldiers to scramble more easily in difficult terrain. Heavier weapons, such as sniper weapon systems, mortars, and machine guns, may need to be attached to the top of rucksacks. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 285

Chapter 11 Improving Steps 11-52. Soldiers are less likely to fall and move more quickly if they have good footing. Hard snow is especially easy to carve steps into and can allow Soldiers to move with less exertion on their calf muscles. Carving steps should be done first in steeper sections and, as time allows, in other areas too. Platforms can also be made where Soldiers are transitioning past intermediate anchors. If a Soldier can easily stand near an intermediate anchor, they can clip around it much faster. This greatly lessens the time required for the group to navigate terrain where objective hazards may be present. Etriers or Slings at Difficult Steps 11-53. The hanging of a sling or etrier (for use as a hand or foothold) where there is a difficult step can help reduce fall potential and increase speed of the group. An etrier is a short ladder that can be made from any piece of rope or cord and creates an artificial step in a place where there is no natural feature to step on. The etrier can be hung off an intermediate anchor or its own anchor. (See figure 11-8.) Caving Ladders 11-54. Manufactured ladders can

cord and creates an artificial step in a place where there is no natural feature to step on. The etrier can be hung off an intermediate anchor or its own anchor. (See figure 11-8.) Caving Ladders 11-54. Manufactured ladders can be useful for large steps and crevasse negotiation. They also enable Soldiers to navigate challenging terrain in the dark, much easier than if they had to search for hand and foot placements. Some are constructed of materials that can be rolled up for transport. While they may make the ascent of a blank wall easier, they are cumbersome to carry. Cables and Via-Ferrata 11-55. If terrain is to be repetitively used for access to higher points for something semi-permanent such as an observation post, it may be in the unit's best interest to build a via-ferrata style system for access. A via-ferrata works similarly to a fixed rope with intermediate anchors, except it uses cable instead of rope. Using cable reduces the need for constant inspection and greatly increases durability. They are much more time consuming to build, but it may be the most feasible option if a unit uses a piece of terrain for an extended period. Given the

reduces the need for constant inspection and greatly increases durability. They are much more time consuming to build, but it may be the most feasible option if a unit uses a piece of terrain for an extended period. Given the cable's rigidity, the attachment method used by Soldiers needs to provide the stretch to lessen fall forces. This equipment can be found on the civilian market. Another component of a via-ferrata-style system is the addition of metal ladder style and foot and handholds. These are for areas and routes that will see traffic over a long time, making the use of soft materials impractical. 286 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Figure 11-8. Etrier styles SECTION II - TYPES OF RAPPELLING 11-56. Rappelling is a method of descending steep terrain using a rope and a means of creating friction to control the rate of descent. This provides Soldiers with a safe way to descend terrain that would otherwise expose them to very high fall risks. 11-57. If the descent distance is greater than a rope length (for example, multipitch), multiple, simple fixed lines can be linked together with anchors at the top and bottom of each rope. Soldiers can then rappel from anchor to anchor and transition from rope to rope until they reach the ground. This method requires many resources and numerous personnel to establish and manage safely. 11-58. Small teams with fewer resources must use the one or two ropes they can carry to rappel the whole group from one anchor to a lower one, then retrieve the rope, and repeat the process until the ground is reached. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 287

Chapter 11 RAPPELLING FUNDAMENTALS 11-59. Rappelling is a quick method of descent, but it can be extremely dangerous. The dangers include anchor failure, equipment failure, and individual error. Carefully select anchors in a mountainous environment. In a mountain environment, take great care to load the anchor slowly and to ensure that no excessive stress is placed on the anchor. To ensure this, prohibit bounding while rappelling; Soldiers should slowly descend. Soldiers should avoid dragging their feet when moving backwards towards the edge as this causes rockfall. 11-60. Soldiers rappelling with weapons should sling them on the back or to the side when wearing packs. Soldiers carrying particularly heavy weapons, such as machine guns, sniper rifles, or mortars may need to strap them to the top of their pack and use additional techniques described below to make rappelling less difficult. RAPPEL SITE SELECTION 11-61. Selecting the rappel point depends on factors, such as mission, cover, route, anchor availability, and edge composition (for example, avoiding those with loose or jagged rocks). The anchor selected should leave no doubt that it will work for its intended purpose. 11-62. Rappel ropes anchored at waist level or above make transitioning over the edge much easier

(for example, avoiding those with loose or jagged rocks). The anchor selected should leave no doubt that it will work for its intended purpose. 11-62. Rappel ropes anchored at waist level or above make transitioning over the edge much easier and reduce the likelihood of Soldiers stumbling or falling. Stumbles and falls are likely to increase the risk of rope damage on sharp rock as well as increase force exerted on anchors. 11-63. Rappel sites with suitable loading and off-loading platforms should be selected. Ideally, they are flat and allow for anchoring far enough away from the edge that Soldiers do not need to be attached to an anchor to prevent accidentally falling off the edge. If this is impossible, use fixed-rope techniques described in section I when approaching the rappel point. A staging area large enough to hold the group in a safe place nearby is also desirable. INSTALLATION CONSIDERATIONS 11-64. The two major factors in deciding how to attach a rappel rope to an anchor are whether the rope needs to be retrievable from the bottom and whether redundancy in rappel rope strands is necessary for safety. Both characteristics cannot be achieved at the same time. 11-65. In

attach a rappel rope to an anchor are whether the rope needs to be retrievable from the bottom and whether redundancy in rappel rope strands is necessary for safety. Both characteristics cannot be achieved at the same time. 11-65. In an operational environment, or during advanced military mountaineering training, ropes must be retrievable. This is because there is presumably no other feasible way to negotiate the vertical obstacle, or the group would be using it. All people and equipment must rappel, and the rope must be recovered for future use. This means that the rope cannot be fixed to the top anchor when the last Soldier begins rappelling. 11-66. When training basic rappelling, retrieving ropes is not necessary. Appropriate rappel sites for inexperienced rappellers should include access between the top and bottom by some other safe means for set up and breakdown. This allows for a greater safety margin by using two fixed independent strands for rappel ropes. Not only does this add redundancy to the system, but also using two strands replicates typical rappelling in an operational environment. 11-67. Anchors that support the maximum force rappellers could exert should be established as described in chapter 9. All rigging should

does this add redundancy to the system, but also using two strands replicates typical rappelling in an operational environment. 11-67. Anchors that support the maximum force rappellers could exert should be established as described in chapter 9. All rigging should be inspected by a qualified advanced military mountaineer, at a minimum. RETRIEVABLE RAPPELS 11-68. Retrievable rappels can be established using appropriate single-point anchors (such as a tree, boulder, horn of rock) using only the rope, or they can be attached to cordelettes, or webbing tied around the anchor feature. If other materials are used, then they cannot be retrieved from the bottom. 11-69. Multipoint anchors require additional materials to establish. This material cannot be retrieved from the bottom. 11-70. The minimum necessary equipment should be used in building retrievable rappel anchors. 288 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Half-Rope Length 11-71. The simplest and most common method is to just run one end of the rope around anchor feature, and then double back stack it until the middle of the rope is around the anchor feature. This ensures both strands are the same length. Tie a stopper knot at the bottom end with both strands leaving 12- to 18-inch tails. This prevents accidentally rappelling off the end of the rope. The ropes are then thrown or back stacked over the edge. 11-72. Sometimes the rope cannot be routed directly around the anchor. The rope can then be back stacked so that the middle of the rope passes through the attachment point for an anchor made from cordelette or webbing or clipped to it using a locking carabiner. 11-73. If a rope could be cut, it is possible to make the system redundant for all but the last rappeller. This system is established in the same manner as above, but once complete a BHK is tied close to the anchor with both strands. This creates two fixed independent strands and adds redundancy to the system. Before the last Soldiers begin to rappel, they simply untie the BHK,

as above, but once complete a BHK is tied close to the anchor with both strands. This creates two fixed independent strands and adds redundancy to the system. Before the last Soldiers begin to rappel, they simply untie the BHK, and the system is retrievable again. Full-Length Rope 11-74. Full-length rappels require two standard-length ropes. Route the end of one rope around or through the anchor point and tie a flat double overhand with the ends of both ropes joining them. Double back stack the ropes and tie a stopper knot as described above. Using a flat overhand to join the rappel ropes reduces the likelihood of the knot being stuck in vegetation of rock features during retrieval. 11-75. Full-length rappels can be made redundant for all but the last rappeller in the same manner as is described above. Rappel Rope Retrieval 11-76. Once all Soldiers have reached the bottom and any stopper knots have been untied, the rope can be retrieved by pulling one strand. The other strand travels up to the anchor and falls. If there are any knots in it, they can become jammed in the anchor and prevent rope retrieval. It is a good idea to

be retrieved by pulling one strand. The other strand travels up to the anchor and falls. If there are any knots in it, they can become jammed in the anchor and prevent rope retrieval. It is a good idea to get excess personnel away from the area prior to pulling in case any loose rocks are dislodged above. 11-77. When pulling the rope on a multipitch rappel, it is a good idea to route the end being pulled through the next anchor, so the rope is less likely to be dropped. RAPPELS WITH FIXED STRANDS 11-78. Whenever a threat of the installation rope being cut is identified, two fixed independent strands should be used. Two strands add redundancy and reduce the likelihood that a fall may occur in a cut rope incident. Installations with two fixed independent strands are typically the standard for rappelling training whether a hazard has been identified. Half-Rope Length 11-79. If using a single anchor, anchor the middle of the rope to it with a bowline knot. If using a preequalized multipoint anchor, tie a fixed loop in the middle of the rope, and attach it to the anchor with two opposing locking carabiners. Full-Rope Length

If using a preequalized multipoint anchor, tie a fixed loop in the middle of the rope, and attach it to the anchor with two opposing locking carabiners. Full-Rope Length 11-80. Anchor the rappel ropes by tying a bowline knot with the top ends of both ropes. 11-81. Situations may arise where the distance of anchors from each other, or the distance of the anchors from the rappel point, requires using a second rope to construct an anchor, or extend the anchor master point closer to the loading platform, allowing for the maximum amount of rope to be utilized for the rappel. In this case, tie a fixed loop with the top ends of both ropes, and clip it to the anchor system master point using two opposing locking carabiners. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 289

Chapter 11 RAPPEL INSTALLATION SPECIAL TECHNIQUES 11-82. There are a few problems that mountaineers should be prepared to solve related to rappelling. The common problems are damaged ropes, short ropes, and the threat of a rope being cut when retrievability is necessary. Damaged Rope 11-83. Ropes occasionally become damaged but may need to be used until they can be replaced following an operation. Mountaineers must be familiar with how to safely use damaged ropes for rappelling. 11-84. First, tie an overhand knot, isolating the damaged spot in the rope. The rope can then continue to be used for many mountaineering tasks. However, the knot in the rope prevents Soldiers from rappelling past. 11-85. If a retrievable rappel is necessary, the damaged rope can be used as follows. The rope is back stacked around the anchor as usual. A fixed bight is tied in the damaged strand near the anchor. That bight is then clipped to the nondamaged strand with a locking carabiner. When loaded, the carabiner fits snug to the anchor like a slip knot. (See figure 11-9.) Both strands of rope are thrown or back stacked off the cliff. 11-86. Soldiers can then rig for rappel using only the

locking carabiner. When loaded, the carabiner fits snug to the anchor like a slip knot. (See figure 11-9.) Both strands of rope are thrown or back stacked off the cliff. 11-86. Soldiers can then rig for rappel using only the nondamaged strand and descend the obstacle. Note. Rappelling on a single strand creates less friction. 11-87. Once all Soldiers have rappelled, the damaged strand, or tagline, can be pulled to retrieve the rope. The nondamaged strand travels up through the carabiner, around the anchor and back down. More care should be taken when pulling the rope because it is more likely to become hung up using this technique. This technique also works when a full-length rappel is necessary and one of the ropes is damaged near the middle. Figure 11-9. Fixed Ropes Short Rope 11-88. Sometimes a group may only have one rope that is not long enough to reach the bottom of a cliff, and the rope cannot be retrieved because the cliff is taller than a half-rope length. 11-89. If the group has enough cordelettes or shorter sections of rope, it can solve the problem. To do so, one end of the rope is lowered until it is on the ground. Cordelettes are then joined by a single strand to the other end until they reach the ground. 11-90. The installation is then rigged to be retrievable with a tagline (as described in paragraphs 11-83 through 11-87, page 290). Soldiers can then rappel on the strand of static rope. When personnel are at the bottom, the end with the cordelettes can be pulled to retrieve the rope. Take more care when pulling the rope because it is more likely to become hung up using this technique. 11-91. Small units can use this technique to reduce the weight of rope they need to carry. Rather than carry two full-sized ropes to rappel a full-rope length, they can carry one rope and a 6- or 7-mm tagline that is cut

units can use this technique to reduce the weight of rope they need to carry. Rather than carry two full-sized ropes to rappel a full-rope length, they can carry one rope and a 6- or 7-mm tagline that is cut the same length from a spool, or plan to use joined cordelettes that are spread out amongst their members. Threat of Cut Rope Using a Retrievable System 11-92. Some situations may require a retrievable rappel, but a threat to the rope is identified (such as sharp rock or falling rock hazard) that cannot be mitigated by simply padding an edge. This problem can be resolved by one of two methods. 11-93. The first involves establishing the retrievable rappel system described above, and then attaching a tube-style device and locking carabiner tight to the anchor. This effectively fixes both strands. All but the last Soldier conducts the rappel with fixed strands. The last Soldier uses the attached device and rappels carefully as normal. This limits the exposure of all but one Soldier to the threat of cut rope. The rope can be pulled from below as previously described. 11-94. The second involves establishing the retrievable rappel system described above, and then

as normal. This limits the exposure of all but one Soldier to the threat of cut rope. The rope can be pulled from below as previously described. 11-94. The second involves establishing the retrievable rappel system described above, and then tying a big knot close to the anchor with both strands fixing them. All but the last Soldier conducts the rappel with fixed strands. The last Soldier unties the knot and rappels carefully as normal. This limits the exposure of all but one Soldier to the threat of cut rope. The rope can be pulled from below as previously described. RAPPELLING TECHNIQUES 11-95. Different situations call for different rappel attachment techniques. They vary in how much friction they produce, the security in which the rappeller is attached to the rope, and whether they allow the rappeller to go hands free. The consequence of falling determines the type of attachment to the rope. Terrain severity determines how much friction is required to control descent. Whether or not other tasks need to be conducted mid-rappel determines the need for a hands-free brake. 11-96. During rappelling, the body generally forms an L-shape with the feet shoulder-width apart, legs straight, and buttocks parallel to

to control descent. Whether or not other tasks need to be conducted mid-rappel determines the need for a hands-free brake. 11-96. During rappelling, the body generally forms an L-shape with the feet shoulder-width apart, legs straight, and buttocks parallel to the ground. When carrying equipment or additional weight, a modified L-shape is used with the legs slightly lower than the buttocks to compensate for the additional weight. The rappeller's back is straight. Rappellers never let go of the ropes with their brake hand until the rappel is complete. Rappellers should keep their feet flat against the surface they are rappelling down and their weight fully on the rope throughout the rappel. Hasty Rappel 11-97. The hasty rappel technique is only used on low-angle slopes. Its primary advantages are that it is simple to learn and execute and requires no specialized equipment. However, take care not to underestimate the terrain being negotiated. Application of this technique in terrain that is too steep can have deadly consequences. The level of rappeller surefootedness determines the severity of terrain for which this technique is appropriate. Gloves can be worn to prevent rope burns. 11-98. Facing slightly sideways to the anchor, rappellers place the ropes horizontally across their back, under their armpits, and palm up. The hand nearest to the anchor is the guide hand, and the other is the brake hand. Bending the rope around the body increases friction. (See figure 11-10, page 292.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 291

Chapter 11 11-99. While moving, Soldiers should keep their legs as perpendicular to the slope as possible, leaning into the rope. This increases the security of foot placements and reduces the likelihood of a slip and fall. 11-100. An experienced Soldier can separate the strands with the brake hand and counter the twist of the rope as it feeds through the hitch to lessen this effect. Chapter 12 Hauling and Lowering Techniques Mountain warfare requires moving Soldiers, weapons, and equipment up, over, and down steep, rugged terrain. It is vital that Soldiers understand the principles and fundamental concepts of hauling and lowering heavy loads both efficiently and safely. SECTION I - HAULING TECHNIQUES 12-1. Mountain operations involve many situations that require hauling systems. A hauling system is a technical rope system used to move a load up steep or vertical terrain comprised of rigging that generates increased mechanical advantage (MA) and captures progress. Properly using hauling systems allows Soldiers to move heavy loads through terrain obstacles that would have been impossible to overcome otherwise. Common situations requiring these systems are equipment recovery, resupply, and rescue operations. Choosing the right system for a given situation requires understanding the principles of MA, categories of systems, and solid judgement. MECHANICAL ADVANTAGE 12-2. A mechanical advantage is a reduction in the force required to move a load, which comes at the cost of time and distance. Specific rope rigging techniques in mountaineering generate mechanical advantage. During hauling operations, MA can be created using a rope through several rigging techniques. The advantage gained reduces the amount of force that is necessary

the cost of time and distance. Specific rope rigging techniques in mountaineering generate mechanical advantage. During hauling operations, MA can be created using a rope through several rigging techniques. The advantage gained reduces the amount of force that is necessary to move a load vertically. This makes hauling heavy loads easier. When choosing and constructing a hauling system, the goal is to use the lowest level of MA to move the load. As MA increases, efficiency and load sensitivity decrease. Efficiency is lost throughout the system anytime the rope touches a surface (including the edge of the cliff), moves through carabiners or pulleys, and rubs on itself in the system. Load sensitivity is the ability of the Soldier pulling on the rope to feel what is happening to the load on the end of the rope. For example, a Soldier pulling a heavy load up a slope by hand will know immediately if the load becomes stuck on an obstacle. However, a Soldier moving the load using a high level of MA would not feel this until there was a large amount of tension in the system. This is important when moving casualties or sensitive equipment. These systems require time,

However, a Soldier moving the load using a high level of MA would not feel this until there was a large amount of tension in the system. This is important when moving casualties or sensitive equipment. These systems require time, materials, and personnel to construct and operate. The intent is not to make easy work of moving the load. The lowest level of MA is desired to maximize load sensitivity, efficiency, and time. 12-3. The more MA a rope system produces, the less efficient it will be. For example, a Soldier operating a 5:1 system only needs to exert 1/5 of the pulling force to move the load. However, that Soldier will need to pull 5 feet of rope through the system for the load to move 1 foot. A balance between work and efficiency must be achieved when selecting an appropriate MA for a given situation. HAULING SYSTEM COMPONENTS 12-4. The hauling system has five basic components. Understanding how they work to move the load together (see the list below) allows Soldiers to achieve greater efficiency during hauling: * Anchors-the anchors required for hauling a heavy load must be unquestionable (see chapter 9). TECHNIQUES TO REDUCE FRICTION 12-13. Friction reduces efficiency of rope movement and can drastically reduce MA. It is important to identify points of friction within the system and strive to reduce them. Efficiency is lost throughout the system anytime the rope touches hardware. Friction can be minimized by using pulleys. Pulleys are used to change direction in rope systems. Pulleys should be small, lightweight, and rated for mountaineering applications. They should accommodate the largest diameter of rope being used. Pulleys are made with several bearings, different-sized sheaves (wheels), and metal alloy side plates. (See figure 12-8, page 310.) Always avoid plastic pulleys. The side plate should rotate on the pulley axle to allow the pulley to be attached at any point along the rope. For best results, the sheave diameter must be at least four times larger than

Always avoid plastic pulleys. The side plate should rotate on the pulley axle to allow the pulley to be attached at any point along the rope. For best results, the sheave diameter must be at least four times larger than the rope's diameter to maintain high rope strength. Pulleys with side plates designed to accommodate prusik knots are referred to as prusik minding pulleys. These pulleys are designed with tolerances that allow the ropes to run through them but block the passage of a prusik hitch, preventing it from being caught in the pulley. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 309

Chapter 12 Figure 12-8. Types of pulleys 12-14. Pulleys are estimated to be approximately 90-percent efficient, while carabiners are considered only 60-percent efficient. The difference between a system that uses pulleys at direction changes and the same system that only uses carabiners is significant. If the team only has a few pulleys, they should be used at the direction changes closest to the system's haul strand. Pulleys in these locations will maximize the force put into the system initially and carry 90-percent efficiency farther through the system. 12-15. Friction also occurs where the mainline contacts the edge of the slope or cliff. If a suitable anchor can be found near the edge, this friction point can be minimized. The mainline can be lifted and routed through a high directional at the top of the slope or cliff to reduce rope contact and friction at the edge. (See figure 12-9.) 310 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

A lowering system is a technical rope system used to move a load down steep or vertical terrain in a controlled fashion using friction hitches or mechanical devices. These sorts of systems are used to control the speed of descent for personnel or equipment using rope. They are an integral part of both highand low-angle rescue. (See chapter 15.) Each new situation will dictate which lowering techniques and systems are appropriate. Understanding basic lowering concepts is key to achieving a safe and efficient solution to the problem. The bottom line for any lowering system is that enough friction must be created to safely control the descent of the load. Different terrain demands different methods of creating friction. When the terrain is steep and broken, selecting a device or technique that provides varying levels of friction is preferred. 12-24. Chapter 13 Mountain Stream Crossing In 480 BC, Persian King Xerxes constructed a pontoon bridge that spanned a mile and a quarter across the Hellespont. After a previous failure to take Greece, the king weighed the options of either finding alternate routes to the north that added months to his expedition or pinpoint potential water crossing locations for his army. Xerxes insisted on the fastest and most direct route across the Aegean inlet for his 300,000 men. While negotiating the linear obstacle involved massive resources and engineering, it would save precious time for his army to reach their objective. SECTION I - MOUNTAIN STREAM FUNDAMENTALS 13-1. A mountain stream crossing is essentially an approach to negotiating a potentially swift and cold waterway that Soldiers may encounter in the mountains. Learning to cross small streams forms a foundation of skills for personnel to manage larger streams and rivers, where consequences could be far more hazardous. 13-2. In an operation involving the crossing of a stream or river, the actual crossing itself is a means, not an end sought. The purpose is for designated units to conduct a crossing to establish security on the far bank to protect remaining personnel. This operation

crossing of a stream or river, the actual crossing itself is a means, not an end sought. The purpose is for designated units to conduct a crossing to establish security on the far bank to protect remaining personnel. This operation should be conducted economically and with minimal loss of momentum. 13-3. There are limits on the safe use of the techniques discussed in this chapter. Not all mountain rivers or streams will be fordable with these techniques. If a water obstacle is too wide, swift, or deep, an alternate route should be used. It may require using aircraft transport if engineer support is unavailable. Reconnaissance of questionable crossing sites is essential. This chapter covers the techniques for crossing mountain streams that have a depth generally not exceeding waist level. 13-4. Stream crossings should not be taken lightly. The force of flowing water may be extremely great and is most often underestimated. All rivers and streams are obstacles to movement. They should be treated as danger areas and avoided whenever possible. When rivers or streams must be crossed, there are many techniques that the small-unit leader may choose from, depending upon the type of stream, its width, speed of the current,

When rivers or streams must be crossed, there are many techniques that the small-unit leader may choose from, depending upon the type of stream, its width, speed of the current, and depth of the water. This activity should be rehearsed prior to execution in the operational environment. RECONNAISSANCE 13-5. Performing a site survey of potential crossing locations (map, photo, or aerial) may not always reveal that a water obstacle exists. In a swamp, for example, unfordable sloughs may not show on the map, and they may be concealed from aerial observation by a canopy of vegetation. 13-6. Site selection is extremely important once Soldiers determine that they must make a crossing. Elevated positions offer an optimal vantage point from which to analyze a large area of possibilities. This is sometimes better than a hundred close views from a riverbank. Select the site selection before the main body arrives and examine the site around a similar time of day that the crossing will be conducted. 13-7. A suitable crossing site should have specific characteristics. A river crossing site should limit exposure to observation, facilitate the installation team crossing (if necessary) or

the site around a similar time of day that the crossing will be conducted. 13-7. A suitable crossing site should have specific characteristics. A river crossing site should limit exposure to observation, facilitate the installation team crossing (if necessary) or swimming with ropes, and minimize drowning hazards. Care must be taken to avoid an installation team crossing upstream of rapids, waterfalls, or fallen trees in the river. For dry features, such as gorges or ravines, the site should facilitate the installation team's descent and ascent crossing while minimizing any falling hazards that exist. While dry crossings are preferred to wet crossings for speed and safety factors, they can become locations for an enemy to place landmines and improvised explosive devices. 13-8. The time of day is an important factor. Recent precipitation or increased temperatures could cause water levels to rise as glaciers or snow-covered peaks begin to melt. Early morning crossings are preferred, as the cooler night temperatures usually reduce the melt from snow and ice. A morning crossing also allows clothing items to dry throughout the day. Whether a crossing is made in daylight or in darkness depends on 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 323

A crossing point should be chosen where the river widens. The sudden width of the channel normally yields a shallow depth. Avoid sharp turns in the river or a narrowing choke point in the river or stream since the water is likely to be deep and have a strong current on the outside of the bend for curves. 13-10. Many mountain streams, especially those fed by glacier runoff, contain sections with numerous braided channels. While often shallower than a main river, this changing landscape offers little in the way of cover and concealment of exposed personnel. Shoals, or partially submerged sandbars, can act like quicksand depending on the riverbed composition. 13-11. Riverbanks should be low enough to accommodate for easy entry and exit from the water.
