Chapter 14 Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue Ten percent of the Earth's land mass is covered by glaciers. Glaciers are rivers of ice flowing under the influence of gravity, constantly restructuring the mountains around them. They often provide the best route in otherwise impassable terrain but can contain crevasses and other hazards that can cause injury, death, or compromise a unit's mission. Soldiers operating in glaciated terrain must understand these hazards, be well versed in the fundamentals of glacier travel, and be proficient with crevasse rescue techniques. SECTION I - GLACIER FUNDAMENTALS 14-1. Glaciers can be large enough to cover an entire continent. They may move only inches or hundreds of feet a year. Movement is caused by gravity, slippage over the bedrock, or by the internal flow in the ice. It is important for route planning and risk management to understand glacial features and understand how they form and move. Dismounted movement across glaciers is hazardous; however, glaciers often provide the easiest passage through more technical terrain on surrounding slopes and faces. GLACIERS 14-2. Glaciers form over time by the weight of accumulating snow compressing older layers of snow into ice. As snow accumulates, gravity takes over and the

provide the easiest passage through more technical terrain on surrounding slopes and faces. GLACIERS 14-2. Glaciers form over time by the weight of accumulating snow compressing older layers of snow into ice. As snow accumulates, gravity takes over and the ice begins to move downhill. The weight of millions of pounds of ice makes a small film of water that acts as a lubricant, enabling it to slide. 14-3. The upper part of the glacier where the annual snow accumulation exceeds the melt is called the accumulation zone. Further down the glacier, the area where melt exceeds accumulation is an area called the ablation zone. The imaginary line between the two zones is known as the firn line. CLASSIFICATION 14-4. There are two classifications of glaciers: alpine glaciers and ice caps. Alpine glaciers form in high mountain bowls. Ice caps can cover thousands of square miles, such as those that cover Greenland and Antarctica. TYPES OF ALPINE GLACIERS 14-5. The following are four types of glaciers: * Valley glacier-resides and flows in a valley. * Cirque glacier-forms and resides in a bowl. These do not advance beyond the bowl. * Hanging glacier-these are a result of valley or cirque glaciers

following are four types of glaciers: * Valley glacier-resides and flows in a valley. * Cirque glacier-forms and resides in a bowl. These do not advance beyond the bowl. * Hanging glacier-these are a result of valley or cirque glaciers flowing and deteriorating. As the movement continues, portions separate and are sometimes left hanging on mountains, ridgelines, or cliffs. * Piedmont glacier-formed by one or more valley glaciers, spreads out into a large area. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 333

Chapter 14 GLACIER OBSTACLES 14-6. Units intending to use glaciers for travel routes must be familiar with their hazards and characteristics to ensure safe and efficient movement on them. Failure to identify and prepare for obstacles, which can come in the form of vertical terrain, can slow or prevent movement. Failure to identify and prepare for hazards can result in significant injury or loss of life. 14-7. Glaciers contain many different features that can impede travel. (See figure 14-1.) They are- * Bergschrund-the bergschrund is a giant crevasse found at the upper limit of glacier movement. It is formed where the moving glacier breaks away from the ice cap or snowfield above. The bergschrund can be high and overhanging and can create an obstacle to movement when moving from the valley floor onto the mountainsides. * Crevasses-crevasses are cracks in the glacier caused by irregularities in the bedrock under the glacier as it moves and flows. Crevasses often form where the angle of the slope increases greatly, causing tension to split open the snow and ice. They also commonly form wherever the glacier makes a turn. They can be transverse, longitudinal, or lateral, depending on their orientation to the direction

the angle of the slope increases greatly, causing tension to split open the snow and ice. They also commonly form wherever the glacier makes a turn. They can be transverse, longitudinal, or lateral, depending on their orientation to the direction of the glacier's movement. Crevasses can be 200-feet deep but are normally 40- to 100-feet deep. Crevasses often hinder travel across glaciers. Snow often conceals crevasses, causing possible major falling hazards to Soldiers. Bypassing them can increase travel time and distance. Snow bridges that form over them can give way without warning. During the summer, the ice is less covered with snow and most crevasses are exposed. They can still be hazardous at night or in reduced visibility. * Moat-the moat is a gap formed where the snow and ice are melted by the warmer rock along the edge of a glacier. The edge of a moat is often undercut. Depending on its size, the moat may be an obstacle to moving on or off the glacier. * Icefalls-icefalls result from the flow of the glacier down a steep ridge. The ridge forces the ice up into a jumbled mass as the glacier flows over the rock. These present formidable

to moving on or off the glacier. * Icefalls-icefalls result from the flow of the glacier down a steep ridge. The ridge forces the ice up into a jumbled mass as the glacier flows over the rock. These present formidable obstacles and should be avoided. * Serac-seracs are ice walls and towers that form in icefalls or on the lower edge of hanging glaciers. They are unstable and can fall unexpectedly. Travel below seracs or hanging glaciers should be avoided when possible. * Nunatak-a nunatak is an island of bedrock that protrudes up through the glacier, creating an obstacle to glacial movement. It creates pressure in the ice that can form crevasses, seracs, and icefalls. * Water hazards-streams that run on the surface and then disappear into a hole are called moulins. Moulins form when meltwater from the glacier finds a crevasse and moves to the ground below the ice. A fall into a moulin can carry a Soldier into the glacier and result in almost certain drowning. The glacial streams above this point must also be treated with respect. They are cold, can be deep, and the slick walls of their channels make them difficult to escape. In the

Chapter 14 ICE AXE AND CRAMPONS 14-12. Ice axes and crampons may be necessary for movement over snow or ice on a glacier but also provide the ability for a Soldier on a rope team to self-arrest to control, stop, and hold the fall of another climber. Ice axes may also be used for snow anchor construction for crevasse rescue. SKIS AND SNOWSHOES 14-13. In deep snow conditions, skis or snowshoes make movement more efficient. They also distribute weight over a greater area when crossing crevasses, which can reduce the likelihood of breaking through a hidden snow bridge. Snowshoes may be more practical than skis for roped glacier travel unless all members of a rope team are skilled skiers. PRUSIKS, SLINGS, AND CORDELETTES 14-14. Short prusik loops, slings, and cordelettes can be used for ascending a rope after a crevasse fall. They are used for belaying rope team members and creating anchors, load transfers, and hauling systems in crevasse rescue. Slings can be used to improvise a chest harness, if necessary, and can be useful to rig the rucksack for removal in the event of a fall. Each Soldier should carry a cordelette, a sling, and a short prusik. SNOW

They can be used while setting up bivouac sites to mark the boundaries of safe areas. They are sometimes useful for whiteout navigation in heavily crevassed terrain. Wands can be made using 4-foot bamboo garden stakes with tape or flagging. OTHER GLACIAL GEAR 14-17. USE OF THE ROPE 14-18. A central question when considering travel over glaciers is whether to use a rope for fall protection. The hazard of hidden crevasses on a glacier varies considerably. In some circumstances, it may be preferable to travel unroped on crevassed glaciers; however, this is not typical. Deciding whether to rope together as a team depends upon the season, mode of travel, snow conditions, and the conditions of the glacier itself. 14-19. Traveling unroped is faster. It makes communication and dissemination of information easier; it can be done with untrained Soldiers. It eliminates the transition times required for tying in and preparing for roped travel. It also allows for movement in tactical formations and a better security posture. 14-20. HAZARD VERSUS CREVASSE HAZARD 14-21. In glaciated terrain, there can be both a risk of falling on steep ground as well as a risk of falling into crevasses. These risks are not managed in the same way. Crevasse hazard is best managed with good route finding and by keeping 8 to 10 meters of rope between Soldiers. Excess slack will cause a Soldier to fall deeper into a crevasse, placing more force on other members of the team and increasing the difficulty of arresting the fall. The falling climber is more likely to hit something or become stuck or wedged. 14-34. A rope with the correct amount of tension lies on the snow with a gentle curve, out of the way of the feet. It can be helpful to hold the rope to the front when traveling downhill and to the rear when traveling uphill. Pace should be adjusted to maintain correct tension in the rope by feel, especially during stops and starts. The Soldier in the lead should set a pace that others can easily follow. 340 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue 14-35. During sharp turns, the rope tends to go slack as the lead Soldier makes a change in the direction of travel, but then it becomes taut as the next Soldier approaches the turn. During turns, team members should adjust pace and keep appropriate tension. New tracks may need to be made outside the leader's footprints to do this. 14-36. As a rope team reaches a rest area or bivouac location, the rope must remain extended until the area has been probed for crevasses. Once it has been deemed safe, the lead member may belay team members into the area by pulling rope through the prusik, with ice axe in hand, ready to self-arrest. Soldiers in the rear may also belay themselves into the location in the same manner. When leaving the location, the same process happens in reverse. (See figure 14-5.) Figure 14-5. Chapter 14 ROUTE FINDING AND CREVASSE DETECTIONS 14-37. Crevasse falls are extremely dangerous, even when traveling roped up with experienced Soldiers. Even when all Soldiers manage the rope well and the fall is stopped immediately, severe injuries can result. Ice axes, crampons, and collapsing snow bridges can cause injuries. Detection and avoidance are the primary skills needed to eliminate the need for crevasse rescue. On heavily crevassed glaciers, it is advisable to use an advanced party to scout and mark the safest route in advance of the main body. This can save hours of wandering, slow progress, and running into dead ends. Once relatively safe routes are established, it can reduce the skill and experience level required of the main body. INFORMATION GATHERING 14-38. Big picture views of the terrain can be very helpful. A maze of crevasses can be analyzed more easily from above than from within. It is a good idea to take digital photos whenever high ground provides a vantage point. Because glaciers move so slowly, crevasse patterns remain constant from year to year, making even old photographs useful for study. Intelligence products or online mapping resources (see appendix B) that contain satellite imagery can provide overhead

provides a vantage point. Because glaciers move so slowly, crevasse patterns remain constant from year to year, making even old photographs useful for study. Intelligence products or online mapping resources (see appendix B) that contain satellite imagery can provide overhead views. These may contain imagery taken during the summer or late season and show the general trends and locations of dense crevasses that may be only partially filled in or have suspect snow bridges when traveling during winter and early season. TIMING 14-39. On snow covered and heavily crevassed glaciers, snow bridges are firmer at night or early in the morning. If stable, they can often provide more direct lines of travel. Warmer daytime temperatures can soften these snow bridges, increasing the likelihood of crevasse fall. This may require finding a longer alternative route. 14-40. Be cautious after snowstorms. Fresh snow can fill in and blend in what might otherwise be detectable crevasses. 14-41. Seasonal timing is equally important. Although unit leaders may not have much say in the time of year they are required to travel on glaciers, a basic understanding of how seasonal changes affect surface conditions is important. Below are descriptions of typical conditions in the midlatitudes:

unit leaders may not have much say in the time of year they are required to travel on glaciers, a basic understanding of how seasonal changes affect surface conditions is important. Below are descriptions of typical conditions in the midlatitudes: * Autumn-in late season conditions, most crevasses are clearly visible and snow bridges have melted out to their maximum extent. Travel is generally safest, as there is little risk of unexpected crevasse fall, but route finding can be difficult and require long detours and lengthy movement times around crevasse fields. In steeper terrain, firm conditions can make falling hazard a higher concern. * Winter-early winter is especially hazardous. Unconsolidated snow hides crevasses but often does not effectively bridge them. Crevasses are more difficult to detect, and unexpected falls are more likely. In late winter, deeper snow conditions may provide more effective snow bridges. Increased snow loads may cause bridges to sag, making detection easier. Skis or snowshoes are often required. * Spring-snowfall has reached its maximum depth, making glacier travel safest. Snow bridges are at their strongest and the snowpack strengthens from warmer weather. Skis or snowshoes are often required, but lines of travel are typically much more direct. *

* Spring-snowfall has reached its maximum depth, making glacier travel safest. Snow bridges are at their strongest and the snowpack strengthens from warmer weather. Skis or snowshoes are often required, but lines of travel are typically much more direct. * Summer-early morning travel on firm snow surfaces makes travel easier, but snow bridges are beginning to weaken. As crevasses open, finding direct routes becomes challenging again. Seracs and icefalls also become more hazardous. 14-42. In some geographical regions further from the poles, these trends can be nearly opposite with surface conditions revolving strictly around dry and rainy seasons. 342 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue ZONES OF TENSION AND COMPRESSION 14-43. Crevasses are formed by tension. Tension is created as glacier ice stretches over rolls in the terrain and where it stretches due to different rates of flow within the glacier. These crevasses form perpendicular to the direction of the stretch. Recognizing where this tension is likely to occur can help with predicting their likely locations when snow fills in or conceals them. Crevasses are more likely at the top of a roll, where the terrain gets steeper and drops away below it. They are also common near the edges of valley glaciers, where additional drag and friction occurs against the valley walls, and the center of the glacier is moving faster. These "marginal" crevasses point toward the center of the glacier at an angle. For this same reason, the centers of glaciers generally have fewer crevasses and are preferred travel routes. 14-44. Compression zones occur where the underlying bedrock flattens out and where glacial ice slows down or piles up. Here, crevasses become narrow and eventually disappear. Glacial ice can also pile up in bowls and flat benches in the terrain and where glaciers flow together. These areas of

flattens out and where glacial ice slows down or piles up. Here, crevasses become narrow and eventually disappear. Glacial ice can also pile up in bowls and flat benches in the terrain and where glaciers flow together. These areas of compression can be relatively crevasse-free. Observing these zones and working to link them together are keys to good route finding. SURFACE CLUES 14-45. Clues to locating crevasses below the surface of the snow can be subtle and difficult to recognize, but it is important for determining an appropriate crossing technique. It can also be just as important to recognize similar clues that do not indicate crevasses and to not waste time and effort on long detours. * Sagging-snow covering larger crevasses gradually deforms and sags under its own weight. Early in the process, this may be barely noticeable, but later the outlines of the crevasse become more defined. Sometimes a slight change in sheen or texture can be observed. Other times, a slight change in color, from dust or windblown snow settling in a subtle depression, can be visible. These should be approached with caution. Snow is, however, an inherently uneven surface, so not every dip, groove, or color change

times, a slight change in color, from dust or windblown snow settling in a subtle depression, can be visible. These should be approached with caution. Snow is, however, an inherently uneven surface, so not every dip, groove, or color change represents a crevasse. In low visibility or flat light, these can be impossible to recognize. * Nearby crevasses-since crevasses are often found in groups and tend to form parallel to one another, look for other crevasses, patterns, or depressions nearby that have similar orientation. * Parallel cracks-in the case of larger crevasses, parallel thin cracks can sometimes form at the edges of a giant snow bridge. Although these can have the appearance of two narrow crevasses, they can be the boundaries of a single, giant snow bridge. PROBING 14-46. Snow probing in areas that look suspicious can be done using an ice axe. It can identify crevasses, determine its true lip, and investigate the extent, length, and width of a crevasse. To probe, the shaft of the axe is thrust into the snow a couple feet ahead of where one moves, looking for a noticeable reduction in resistance. If there is a sudden drop in resistance, there is likely a

crevasse. To probe, the shaft of the axe is thrust into the snow a couple feet ahead of where one moves, looking for a noticeable reduction in resistance. If there is a sudden drop in resistance, there is likely a crevasse, but it can also be a soft snow layer. Probing requires experience to accurately interpret. The short length of an ice axe makes this difficult. Avalanche probes and ski poles with the basket removed are better choices, if available. Probing is also required for determining safe bivouac locations. CROSSING TECHNIQUES 14-47. There are a variety of options and techniques for crossing crevasses, and leaders must understand and be capable of incorporating any combination of them to adapt to the terrain. Rope teams should travel perpendicular to the direction of crevasses to reduce the risk of exposing more than one Soldier at a time. (See figure 14-6, page 344.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 343

Chapter 14 Figure 14-6. Crossing perpendicular to crevasses End Running 14-48. There is no guarantee as to the dependability of snow bridges. Sometimes it is preferable to cross at one end of a crevasse where its width narrows, rather than take a chance with a snow bridge. (See figure 14-7.) With large crevasses, this could lead to traveling a quarter of a mile or more to gain 30 feet of forward progress. In winter or spring, seasonal snow may still cover the narrow ends of a crevasse. What looks like the end of the crevasse might not be its actual end. This assessment can require some judgement. Make a wide swing, probe carefully, and cross at a right angle to the crevasse. 344 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue Figure 14-7. End running crevasses Using a Snow Bridge 14-49. When end running is not practical, use snow bridges to cross. (See figure 14-8.) Always attempt to get a look at the crevasse from the side before committing to it, and probe when approaching the lip. The remaining Soldier in the team provides a moving belay by controlling the slack and remaining ready to self-arrest. Once the leader is across, the rest of the team must follow exactly in the leader's footsteps. At this point, the leader controls slack and remains prepared for self-arrest. Prusiks can be used here to manage slack in the rope during this process as well. If there is doubt as to one's ability to stop a fall, a fixed belay must be constructed with a snow or ice anchor. Chapter 14 Jumping 14-50. Only conduct jumping when the gap is short. Running leaps requiring big push offs from suspect crevasse lips and falls can result in serious injury. Jumping should not be attempted unless there are no other options. Enough slack must be provided for the jumper to clear the crevasse without question. Be wary of catching a crampon and use common sense. Climbing into the Crevasse 14-51. Occasionally, it may be practical to climb down into a shallow crevasse and climb back out the other side. Standard belay techniques (see chapter 10) should be used. Be especially aware of bottoms that appear solid but are not. Echelon Formation 14-52. When it is impractical to travel perpendicular to existing crevasses and Soldiers must travel parallel, the echelon formation can be used. (See figure 14-9.) This keeps team members still to the rear but offset slightly to the side. This provides an alternative to following the leader's tracks in a single-file line. This should only be used on heavily crevassed sections where all crevasses are visible and there is very little risk of falling into a hidden one. Figure 14-9. Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue CREVASSE FALL CONSIDERATIONS 14-54. Mutually supporting rope teams should have a minimum of one Soldier per team who is trained in crevasse rescue. This will ensure that rescue capability can always be provided, even when the more experienced member of another rope team is the one to fall in. Two trained Soldiers are necessary in rope teams traveling independently, away from supporting teams. 14-55. Crevasse falls are rarely dramatic and sudden falls that rip team members off their feet and result in someone dangling down inside an abyss. In fact, most crevasse falls involve breaking through a snow bridge but falling no further than waste deep, and with minimal force exerted on team members. Despite this, Soldiers must be trained to deal with more severe falls and be able to adapt and adjust to a variety of circumstances. Options for crevasse rescue involve an abundance of variables. They depend largely upon the breakdown of rope teams, the number of Soldiers per rope, conditions of the glacier, and specific equipment carried. A comprehensive and detailed description of crevasse rescue techniques is well beyond the scope of this publication. Instead, the steps and decision process typically used

A comprehensive and detailed description of crevasse rescue techniques is well beyond the scope of this publication. Instead, the steps and decision process typically used for a three-person rope team are described below. STEPS TO TAKE FOR CREVASSE FALL 14-56. The following steps should be considered in the event of a crevasse fall with a three-person rope team. STOP THE FALL 14-57. Stop the fall immediately. Some falls may be barely noticeable, while others may require dropping into the self-arrest position in the opposite direction. Stopping falls on firm surfaces can be more difficult than soft ones. Once the fall is arrested, both rescuers should kick crampon points into the snow to establish a strong, stable position to prevent the victim from slipping any further. Communication can often be made with the victim at this point. In circumstances where Soldiers have only fallen a few feet or are stuck in the snow bridge, they may be able to climb out unassisted. If a Soldier is not able to quickly self-recover, then the following steps must be taken. (See figure 14-10, page 348.) 26 November 2025

Chapter 14 Figure 14-10. Stopping a crevasse fall CONSTRUCT AN ANCHOR AND TRANSFER THE LOAD 14-58. When another rope team is available, then they can construct an anchor and help the team transfer the load of the fallen Soldier onto it. (See figure 14-11.) Otherwise, the Soldier on the opposite end is usually the one to complete this step. End Soldiers slowly get out of the self-arrest, making sure that middle Soldiers can still hold the weight. End Soldiers establish an anchor (see chapter 9 for snow and ice anchors) below the middle climber and towards the crevasse. They attach a prusik to the loaded rope and clip it to the anchor with a locking carabiner. If there is limited distance between the middle climber and the crevasse lip, the anchor can be constructed above the middle climber. In this case, the slack rope itself, between the middle and end climber can be used to attach directly to the anchor. 348 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue 14-59. Next, the end Soldiers get back into the self-arrest position to back up middle Soldiers as they transfer the weight of fallen Soldiers onto this prusik. Once pressure is relieved from middle Soldiers, it is common for them to continue backing up this anchor while the end climber improves it or constructs additional components. This anchor must be unquestionably strong, as it may be used to haul the Soldier out. The prusik should also be backed up with a suitable knot clipped to the anchor. Figure 14-11. Construct the anchor and transfer the load COMMUNICATE WITH THE FALLEN CLIMBER AND MAKE A PLAN 14-60. To make a clear assessment and develop a plan, it is best to approach the edge of the crevasse where the fallen Soldier can be seen and heard. This can be done by one of the team members using a safety prusik attached to the unweighted portion of the rope. Exercise caution approaching the edge. Determination of what to do next will depend on how far down the climbers are, whether they sustained injuries, extent of any injuries, and characteristics of the terrain in and around the crevasse. The loaded

Exercise caution approaching the edge. Determination of what to do next will depend on how far down the climbers are, whether they sustained injuries, extent of any injuries, and characteristics of the terrain in and around the crevasse. The loaded rope can often become entrenched into the lip of the crevasse, complicating rescue options. This may be a good time to pad underneath the rope to prevent this from becoming worse with an ice axe shaft, foam pad, or rucksack slid underneath the rope as close to the edge as can be reached. This can take some work, and items used for padding should be anchored so that it cannot fall into the crevasse. Various options for rescue are described below. Self-Rescue 14-61. Self-rescue can be achieved by the fallen climber ascending the rope itself using a prusik ascent (see paragraphs 11-39 through 11-49, pages 282 through 284) or other techniques discussed in chapter 11 and is also shown in figure 14-10, page 348. When possible, this is often the easiest and fastest option. The prusik ascent prevents the fallen Soldier from becoming cold waiting for rescuers. Getting the weight of the rucksack off the body and onto the rope

figure 14-10, page 348. When possible, this is often the easiest and fastest option. The prusik ascent prevents the fallen Soldier from becoming cold waiting for rescuers. Getting the weight of the rucksack off the body and onto the rope is also particularly helpful for staying upright. Assistance from team members may be required to surmount the crevasse lip. The method does not work if the fallen Soldier sustained significant injuries. Belay 14-62. Belays may be a fast, easy option when crampons and ice axes can be used to climb out of the hole, especially if or when the rope is too entrenched in the crevasse lip to prusik out. The remaining free end of the rope can be passed down to the fallen climber to tie into the harness with, while a team member above creates a belay at the anchor. Again, if the fallen Soldier is injured, this method may not be possible. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 349

Chapter 14 Haul 14-63. If none of the above options are viable, a more complex solution of hauling the fallen climber out will be needed. HAULING 14-64. Hauling techniques used for MA described in chapter 12 may be used for hauling; however, there are circumstances specific to working with crevasses that must be considered. Direct Haul 14-65. This refers to hauling systems constructed on the fallen climber's weighted strand of rope. A common example is the 3:1 hauling system. (See figure 12-4, page 307.) This is constructed by untying the backup knot behind the prusik and using this remaining rope to construct the system. A disadvantage to the direct haul is that it does not work if the rope is entrenched in the crevasse lip. This method is also impractical if there are knots tied in the weighted rope to help hold the crevasse fall. (See figure 14-12.) Figure 14-12. Direct haul using a 3:1 hauling system 350 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue Drop Loop 14-66. Drop loops refer to hauling systems that use a bight of rope sent down and attach to the fallen climber's harness, independent of the climber's weighted strand. (See figure 14-13.) An example is the 2:1 hauling system. (See figure 12-3, page 307.) This is often the preferred method because the crevasse lip can be padded prior to hauling and because the victim can often assist by pulling on the strand opposite the haul strand. Drop-loop hauls do require victims to clip the bight of rope into the harness, so in the case of an unconscious victim, this step may need to be done by first rappelling to them then re-ascending. Drop-loop systems can be performed using the remainder of the rope or by a separate rope team utilizing a different rope altogether. Progress must still be captured during the haul for safety. This may be done by pulling rope through the prusik on the original tensioned rope. Figure 14-13. Drop-loop rescue system (2:1) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 351

Chapter 14 SECTION IV - TRAINING 14-67. Even when mutually supporting rope teams are used, good route finding, and crevasse detection skills are critical. Every rope team must have at least one Soldier with solid crevasse rescue skills. Commanders cannot just hope for seasonally low-risk conditions, nor can they rely solely on advanced parties or recon teams to consistently find routes that are passable without the need for ropes. A lack of expertise can leave units with a large capability gap. 14-68. Training and experience in glacier travel are most productive when conducted on glaciers. Most glaciated terrain in the lower 48 states is in the Pacific Northwest. The high cost of travel and time commitments to access them make training plans difficult for units to execute. This makes it inconvenient even for units located at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington. In the absence of glaciated terrain, units can still conduct simulated training exercises focusing on the basic strategies for roping up and preparing individual and team equipment. Chapter 15 Mountain Rescue and Evacuation A unit's capability to conduct mountain rescue and evacuation is a critical part of mountain operations. Swift and efficient rescue can mean the difference between success and failure of a mission or even the survival of a casualty. In mountainous terrain, even relatively minor injuries may require evacuation. The type of injury, distance to be moved, terrain, training level of the team, and litter capabilities determine the evacuation technique chosen. Air evacuation is preferred. However, the weather, tactical situation, or operational ceiling of the aircraft may make this impossible. Therefore, it is imperative that all personnel are trained in mountain evacuation techniques and are self-sufficient. Casualties should be triaged before evacuation. The most experienced medical personnel available perform triage (physician, physician's assistant, or medic). SECTION I - RESCUE OPERATIONS 15-1. Every commander should have a MEDEVAC plan before undertaking an operation. This plan should have dedicated assets (primary, alternate, contingency, and emergency) in place so as not to rely on a single evacuation platform or method. Rotary-wing aircraft may be available to remove casualties from cliffs or inaccessible sites and to quickly transport casualties to a medical treatment facility. However, high altitudes and gusting

so as not to rely on a single evacuation platform or method. Rotary-wing aircraft may be available to remove casualties from cliffs or inaccessible sites and to quickly transport casualties to a medical treatment facility. However, high altitudes and gusting winds reduce the ability of fixed-wing or rotary-wing aircraft to assist in operations. Therefore, relying solely on aircraft or specialized equipment is a poor substitute for careful planning. 15-2. The two types of rescue operations encountered by units operating in mountainous environments are deliberate and improvised. DELIBERATE 15-3. Deliberate rescue is when the mission objective itself is a rescue operation, thus allowing time for focused planning and the use of specialized rescue specific equipment. IMPROVISED 15-4. Improvised rescue situations are encountered when a casualty is sustained during normal operations and conducting a rescue was not the intended objective. Even improvised rescue operations should be practiced and rehearsed to minimize the negative effects on mission capability. All operations should have a CASEVAC plan developed before an emergency arises (plan for the worst and hope for the best). Ensure that the MEDEVAC plan is well thought out and comprehensive. CASEVAC plan developed before an emergency arises (plan for the worst and hope for the best). Ensure that the MEDEVAC plan is well thought out and comprehensive. These plans must be understood by all who may be involved in a potential rescue. PLANNING 15-5. The rescue tasks must be identified by obtaining the following information: * Number of casualties by precedence (urgent, priority, routine, convenience). * Number of casualties by type (litter or ambulatory) and the nature of their injuries. * Terrain features and with respect to the location of the casualties. * Tactical situation. * Any assets available to aid in security, rescue, treatment, and evacuation. * If treatment can be provided at the scene or if the casualty requires movement to a safer location. * Additional personnel or equipment required for the rescue operation. * Any circumstances that may require specialized skills. * Weather conditions. * Difficulty of the terrain. * Time available. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 353

In some cases, trained personnel and equipment available for low- or high-angle rescue may allow for safer, less physically demanding operations. A lack of these resources and capabilities may require traveling longer distances around steeper terrain, greatly increasing the burden on rescuers. CONSIDERATIONS 15-7. Time considerations can cause a leader to compromise planning stages or treatment (beyond first aid). Make a realistic estimate of time available as quickly as possible to determine the action time remaining. The key elements are the casualty's condition and ability to endure the environment. Even a mild rain can complicate an otherwise simple rescue. In higher altitudes, extreme cold or strong winds can greatly increase the rescue's time and complexity. GENERAL STEPS 15-9. Mountain Rescue and Evacuation essential. Once formal evacuation training has been received, proficiency can be maintained by periodic integration with other concurrent training exercises. Scenarios that require simple casualty movement techniques, with and without litters, as well as low-angle slope evacuations (see section II) can easily be created. Scenarios are added when time becomes available during or following other training exercises. These opportunities allow commanders to quickly evaluate a unit's preparedness to carry out basic rescues if needed, refresh level 1 skills, and help to reinforce unit teamwork and problem solving. Basic military mountaineers, at a minimum, should oversee this training. Medical personnel should be present. Rescues in complex 4th- and 5th-class terrain, whether real or simulated, require advanced-level training and skills, and they must be led by level 2 and level 3 mountaineers. PROLONGED FIELD CARE 15-11. The mountain environment is defined by austere and remote conditions. This environment, combined with the difficulty of patient movement, creates situations that can extend patient management over many hours or days. Prolonged field care is the continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement beyond the holding capability of that role of care (JP 4-02). 15-12. Medical personnel with standard training

can extend patient management over many hours or days. Prolonged field care is the continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement beyond the holding capability of that role of care (JP 4-02). 15-12. Medical personnel with standard training may be required to perform beyond their skillset. Specific training should be conducted to prepare medical and nonmedical personnel for prolonged field care situations. Tactical combat casualty care uses protocols aimed primarily at preventing mortality in the first few hours of treatment, prior to arrival at surgical resuscitative care. However, patients in the mountains lacking fast and immediate evacuation are often at risk for complications, such as sepsis, multi-organ system failure, respiratory compromise, and other serious conditions. Prolonged field care begins with the sound principles of tactical combat casualty care, but when care is extended over hours or days, treatment must continuously be re-evaluated. Diligence is necessary to minimize the effect of potentially harmful interventions and to prevent, recognize, and treat conditions that may develop over time. 15-13. Critical patients ultimately require care in a hospital with surgery, blood products, an intensive care unit, and advanced imaging. Casualties in the mountains can be moved and transported in a variety of ways, from simple manual field carries to high-angle evacuations using litters and complex rope systems. The type of injury, distance to be moved, time available, and resources will determine the best technique for a given situation. MOVING CASUALTIES WITHOUT LITTERS 15-15. There are varieties of circumstances where casualties may move, be moved, or be carried without the use of litters. This could be a result of sustaining relatively minor injuries, not having a litter available, or not having the available personnel for litter transport. Alternatively, these could involve moving a casualty in technical terrain that is not suited for transport in a litter. If casualties are able, they can walk, with one or more rescuers walking alongside, to provide physical support. A rescuer close behind can help in difficult terrain. Casualties can also be placed in a seat or improvised harness and lowered or hauled through steep terrain using the techniques described in chapter 12. This may be done with ambulatory patients or may be necessary in situations where an injured Soldier must be moved from a cliff to an alternate location where packaging in a litter is more easily accomplished. This may require considerable assistance from rescuers or other Soldiers. It should only be attempted when necessary and after any immediate life-threatening injuries have been treated. Remember the more complex the technical rope systems become, the more time consuming they tend to be, increasing exposure and vulnerability to enemy attack. MOVING CASUALTIES IN LITTERS 15-21. Usually, casualties with significant injuries in the mountains need to be evacuated with the use of a litter. Several types of litters are available for transporting casualties in rough terrain. 358 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Rescue and Evacuation MANUFACTURED LITTERS 15-22. The following litters are readily available to mountaineering units: * The poleless, nonrigid litter is lightweight and readily available but is the least favored litter. It does little to protect the patient's injuries and is not appropriate for attachment to any rope system. * The standard collapsible litter is readily available in all units and may be rigged for movement over rough mountainous terrain. However, it is not suitable for carry as a contingency litter due to its bulk and weight. * A rigid, metal-framed, basket-style litter that is rated for hoist operations is very well-suited for moving casualties through mountainous environments. These litters provide excellent patient protection and spinal immobilization, and when rigged properly, can readily attach to a variety of technical rope systems. The drawbacks to this type of litter are that it is heavy and is not designed to slide over surfaces. A single-wheel attachment is available, which vastly increases the efficiency of movement over moderate terrain but comes at the cost of an even greater weight to be carried. * The patient rescue and recovery collapsible litter system is a lightweight, semirigid, rollout plastic litter that can also be

the efficiency of movement over moderate terrain but comes at the cost of an even greater weight to be carried. * The patient rescue and recovery collapsible litter system is a lightweight, semirigid, rollout plastic litter that can also be rigged to meet rating requirements for hoist operations. The most commonly issued and used version in mountaineering is the rescue litter, which provides excellent patient support and protection. This is the preferred litter for mountain operations due to its versatility and relatively low weight. However, it is not a spinal immobilization device. A backboard must be used with this system for patients who have injuries to the shoulder area. This system will accommodate long and short backboards, scoop stretchers, and most other immobilization equipment. IMPROVISED LITTERS 15-23. Litters can be improvised in the field using several techniques, but all of them require construction materials and time, generally offer less patient protection, and are more prone to breakage. 15-24. Litters can be made by securing poles inside blankets, tarps, ponchos, jackets, shirts, sacks, or bags. Casualties must be packaged and secured to litters before movement in rough terrain. Proper packaging should achieve stabilization, immobilization, protection from hypothermia, and preparation for transport. Physically strapping a person into a litter is relatively easy but making it comfortable and effective can be a challenge. The needs of litter bound casualties are great and should not be overlooked or underestimated. The decisions made during initial packaging will affect the physical and mental outcomes for the casualty in the end. 15-27. Chapter 15 15-29. Consider protecting the insulating layers from casualties themselves if there is a possibility they could become incontinent. A trash bag or waterproof bag with leg holes cut in it can be filled with socks or T-shirts to form a diaper. Wrap the casualty as completely as possible, leaving only necessary areas exposed. When available, hot water bottles should be added and placed by the casualty's axillary areas (armpits, groin) and the neck to provide active rewarming. MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES 15-30. ATP 4-02.13 covers general principles of handling and moving with litters-principles that apply in all terrain. However, in rugged mountainous terrain, teams must often move considerably slower. Extensive personnel may be required to ensure adequate rest and safety. Advanced teams may be useful for route selection and clearing. 15-31. For longer movements, it can be useful to add slings or cordelettes to the litter rim or handles for each litter bearer. These slings can be passed over the shoulders to the opposite hand, allowing each bearer to push down with the hand opposite the litter. This can help to reduce strain on the arm and hand carrying the litter, as well as providing some height adjustment. 15-32. In

This can help to reduce strain on the arm and hand carrying the litter, as well as providing some height adjustment. 15-32. In severely uneven terrain, such as talus or boulder fields, the pass-through technique can make movement safer for both the casualty and rescuers, provided extra personnel are available. To conduct the pass-through technique, simply have extra litter bearers take up static positions in the terrain ahead of the litter and as close to one another as possible. The litter is then passed forward into the hands of the extra litter bearers. As soon as litter bearers in the rear become obsolete, they move around and take up a new position further ahead in the direction of travel. They then wait until the litter reaches them and repeat the technique. This allows rescuers to remain still as the litter is transported, taking advantage of secure footing and stable positions. In this way, the litter is less likely to be dropped and litter bearers are less likely to sustain an injury attempting to move and carry the heavy load at the same time.

Mountain Rescue and Evacuation LOW-ANGLE RESCUE 15-35. Low-angle rescue can generally be categorized by roped litter evacuations on low to moderately steep slopes where much of the weight of the casualty and rescuer is still supported by the ground. In this terrain, the litter slides along the slope, either up or down, depending on the direction of travel. The rope pathway should be cleared prior to casualty movement. All precautions must be taken to keep the litter within the fall line of gravity to eliminate pendulum swings. In all situations, the rescue team should strive to solve the terrain problem safely with the least technical solution. ROPE ATTACHMENT 15-36. Rescue litters are generally oriented vertically during low-angle slope evacuations. (See figure 15-5.) The rescue rope is attached to a vertical attachment point at the head of the litter with a locking carabiner or carabiners. The rope is connected at the head of the litter for comfort and for ensuring that blood does not pool at the casualty's head during transport. 15-37. In some situations, the rescue rope can be used to simply provide a tight belay for the casualty while litter teams carry a litter up or down slopes. ATTENDANTS 15-40. In steeper terrain where lowering or raising the litter from above is necessary, there is often a falling hazard for the litter team. If rescuers cannot safely walk beside the litter, it is typically advisable to use a single rescuer attached to the system as an attendant. This attendant's primary responsibility is to ensure the litter and casualty do not roll over, become hung up on terrain obstacles, or create slack in the system. 15-41. The litter and attendant can be lowered using various lowering techniques described in chapter 12. Select or construct extremely solid anchors, tie off the end of the rope to close the system, and apply appropriate hands-free backups. The rope pathway should be cleared prior to casualty movement, and all precautions must be taken to keep the litter within the fall line of gravity to eliminate pendulum swings. A Soldier secured safely near the edge can often be helpful to relay commands and help control the speed of the lower. Avoid rope pathways with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential. 15-45. Chapter 15 RAISING 15-46. The litter and attendant can be raised through steep terrain using the various hauling techniques described in chapter 12. This could be done by a hauling team from above using main force or by creating MA using one of the systems previously described. If using main force, a prusik or other friction hitch should be attached to the rope and anchored as a progress capture. An additional member on the haul team must be dedicated to managing the prusik during this method. If using MA, the hauling team must pull slow and steady and should be extremely aware of the loss of feel for the load. In either case, the rope pathway should be cleared prior to casualty movement, and all precautions must be taken to keep the litter within the fall line of gravity to eliminate pendulum swings. A Soldier secured safely near the edge can often be helpful to relay commands and help control the speed of the haul. Avoid hauling in terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential. HIGH-ANGLE RESCUE 15-47. High-angle rescue generally refers to roped evacuations down steep cliffs and 5th-class terrain. High-angle rescue requires formal training, experience, excellent judgement, and good technical problem-solving skills. It often requires a substantial amount of time. Only level 2 and 3 military mountaineers should only conduct high-angle rescue, when necessary. There are often many variables involved in high-angle rescue, and thus, there is no prescriptive set way to deal with the many challenges that can be encountered. Because a combination of skills and techniques may ultimately be required, including climbing techniques, belays, rappels, hauling and lowering methods, or even the use of high lines, a comprehensive focus is well beyond the scope of this training circular. Rather, this section will focus on some of the fundamental principles and commonly used tools and techniques. LITTER RIGGING 15-48. Whether a rescue litter or a rigid metal basket is used for a high-angle evacuation, the rigging is similar. The litter can be rigged for horizontal orientation, like a helicopter hoist configuration, or it can be rigged for a vertical orientation the same as

or a rigid metal basket is used for a high-angle evacuation, the rigging is similar. The litter can be rigged for horizontal orientation, like a helicopter hoist configuration, or it can be rigged for a vertical orientation the same as described for lower-angle evacuations. In many cases, it is ideal to package the casualty in a manufactured or improvised harness. This allows the harness to connect to the rope system independently of the attachment to the litter itself. This can also be achieved with webbing using a variety of techniques. Horizontal Orientation 15-49. Horizontal orientation of the litter is often used in cases where the nature of the injury makes vertical orientation unsuitable, such as spinal, pelvic, and lower leg injuries. (See figure 15-8.) Severely hypothermic and cardiac patients should also be kept as horizontal as possible during transport. The rescue litter comes with two hoist straps that can be used for this. In the case of a similar metal basket litter, cordage or webbing can be rigged to connect the four corners to a single midline attachment point. (See figure 15-9.) Ensure the head end of the litter is slightly higher than the foot end, about 6 inches when

basket litter, cordage or webbing can be rigged to connect the four corners to a single midline attachment point. (See figure 15-9.) Ensure the head end of the litter is slightly higher than the foot end, about 6 inches when unloaded. Use locking carabiners and ensure that all carabiners used in the rigging are oriented correctly. It is easy to create a dangerous situation by cross-loading carabiners. 364 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Rescue and Evacuation Figure 15-8. Litter rigged horizontal orientation with hoist straps Figure 15-9. Basket litter rigged for horizontal orientation Vertical Orientation 15-50. Vertical litter orientation is often preferred as it can make for a simpler and more fluid edge transition. It is also lower profile, protects the patient better from rockfall and other hazards, and does not require a change in rope attachment point when transitioning to or from low-angle terrain. However, this method can be unsuitable for casualties with spinal, pelvic, and some lower leg injuries and requires securing the patient in such a way to minimize movement in the litter once evacuation begins. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 365

Chapter 15 ROPE SELECTION 15-51. Rope rescue systems should meet the industry standard 10:1 static system safety factor (SSSF). Calculate the SSSF by first determining the force created by the rescue load. Each person attached to the system is estimated to create 1 kN. Therefore, one casualty and one rescuer are estimated to be a 2-kN load. For a 2-kN load, all components of the rescue system must be rated to 20-kN breaking strength to meet the 10:1 SSSF requirement. In this case, ropes would require a minimum breaking strength of around 30 kN to account for an estimated 1/3 strength loss when knots are tied into the rope. Most static kernmantle ropes 11 mm in diameter meet this 30 kN threshold. However, for mountain rescue operations, it is much more practical to use lighter weight ropes that can more easily be carried, allow for faster response times, and function better with other components of the mountaineering kits. These may have MBSs that are a little less than 30 kN, but the advantages often outweigh the risks of encroaching on the very robust 10:1 SSSF. More important than the strength of a thinner diameter rope, users must be cognizant of

have MBSs that are a little less than 30 kN, but the advantages often outweigh the risks of encroaching on the very robust 10:1 SSSF. More important than the strength of a thinner diameter rope, users must be cognizant of edge abrasion issues. These ropes should be static (low stretch) and should have a minimum diameter of 9.5 mm and a minimum breaking strength of 26 kN. 15-52. Rescues can be carried out using single or tandem rope systems. Single Rope 15-53. Single rope technique, much like that described for use with low-angle rescue, is typically simpler to construct and operate, and generally requires less equipment overall. However, it does not include redundancy for system or rope failure. Equipment breakage or human error can have catastrophic results. Consider using this technique only when there is no prominent edge transition, no sharp rock edges on the pitch, and time and resources are limited. Tandem Rope 15-54. Tandem rope technique is more complex and time consuming, and gear intensive to construct. However, it has the added benefit of built-in redundancy against system or rope failure or human errors in rigging and operation. Consider tandem rope systems when there are prominent or difficult

complex and time consuming, and gear intensive to construct. However, it has the added benefit of built-in redundancy against system or rope failure or human errors in rigging and operation. Consider tandem rope systems when there are prominent or difficult edge transitions due to the potential for high-peak forces in the event of failure, sharp rock edges, or when there is limited team experience regarding the rigging of anchors and lowering or belay systems. 15-55. Tandem rope technique uses two separate ropes referred to as the main line and the belay line. Each rope system requires a separate anchor. The main line is used to haul or lower the litter, and the belay line is there in case of main line failure. 15-56. The two ropes are connected to the litter attachment point with interlocking long tailed bowlines. (See figure 15-10.) The tail or free end of each bowline is used as a secondary attachment point for the patient and the litter attendant. 366 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Sites suitable for lowering should have solid anchor points, good loading and unloading platforms, and good clearance for the casualty along the route. Terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential should be avoided when lowering is necessary. The litter and attendant can be lowered using various lowering techniques described in chapter 12, but techniques that generally provide greater friction are preferred. The end of the rope should be tied off to close the system. RAISING 15-59. Sites suitable for hauling should have solid anchor points, good loading and unloading platforms, and good clearance for the casualty along the route. Terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential should be avoided when hauling is necessary. The litter and attendant may be hauled using techniques described in chapter 12. Systems with higher ratios may be necessary, as well as redirection and piggyback techniques. BELAY LINE 15-60. While a properly constructed main line and solid anchor system should not fail, there is potential for a severe shock to the system if the attendant slips going over the edge. If such a slip occurs, the shock load will

While a properly constructed main line and solid anchor system should not fail, there is potential for a severe shock to the system if the attendant slips going over the edge. If such a slip occurs, the shock load will be significant due to the short amount of rope available to absorb the force, and the static nature of all the system components. The separate belay line is also here for this purpose. If a high directional is used, the belay line should not be routed through it. This would cause a greater fall distance before the belay line could catch the load in the event of failure or breakage of the high directional. 15-61. While there are manufactured devices available that meet the criteria for a technical rescue belay, the simplest and most field expedient method is called the tandem prusik belay. Two prusiks, preferably made from 7- or 8-mm nylon static utility cord are tied approximately 2-inches apart on the belay line. The length of the prusik closer to the anchor should be a few inches shorter than the other prusik. These prusiks are then attached to the belay anchor with a locking carabiner. To use the belay,

A high-angle rescue requires a skilled team to be conducted. The following positions are a bare minimum and mandatory for a safe evacuation. Team Leader 15-63. The team leader has overall responsibility for the operation. The team leader considers all available options and selects the most appropriate technique for the situation. The team leader makes judgments based on the nature or urgency of the injury, the tactical situation, the nature of the terrain, and the personnel and resources available. should be the spokesperson to keep communications clear. Typically, the main line team is responsible for anchor construction and hauling system rigging. Edge Safety 15-66. The edge safety keeps the edge area clean of debris, places edge protection if necessary, and assists the load over the edge during the transition. The edge safety also relays commands between the attendant and the personnel above. During difficult edge transitions, two edge safeties may be used. Attendant 15-67. This litter attendant manages the handling of the patient and litter during the technical portion of the rescue. Often the primary focus of the attendant is making sure that the litter is protected and keeping slack out of the system. These often require pulling the litter out away from the terrain for smooth lowers or raises. This is considerably taxing and may require having an adjustable length attachment to the rope system. The litter attendant should have both primary and secondary attachment points for redundancy. The litter attendant determines and adjusts the rate of litter movement up or down as necessary. Chapter 16 Rope Bridges Operations in mountainous terrain often encounter obstacles, such as fast flowing water, ravines, or rock fields. Well-trained mountaineers can exploit this terrain with the use of rope bridges and high lines. These allow units to take the terrain out of the equation by using a rope suspended in the air to cross the obstacle. High lines are a type of rope bridge. The two terms are often used synonymously, and the techniques are relatively interchangeable; however, for the purposes of this training circular, we will refer to rope bridges when used for assisting personnel for river crossings and the term "high lines" to denote rope installations used to span longer or higher gaps in terrain. SECTION I - TECHNIQUES 16-1. A rope bridge is a rope tensioned between two anchors and suspended off the ground to assist units with crossing rivers. These are sometimes necessary in situations with swift and dangerous currents or very cold water, where keeping the majority of Soldiers dry is important. 16-2. Rope bridges can pose distinct disadvantages. Though linear in nature, rope bridge crossings in a tactical environment should be considered VDAs. This is because units establishing and using them are

where keeping the majority of Soldiers dry is important. 16-2. Rope bridges can pose distinct disadvantages. Though linear in nature, rope bridge crossings in a tactical environment should be considered VDAs. This is because units establishing and using them are fixed and potentially split by the river obstacle for prolonged periods. This can put them at a significant tactical disadvantage. (See ATP 3-21.50 for more VDA-crossing considerations.) CONSTRUCTION 16-3. The rope bridge is constructed using a static rope. The rope is anchored on the far side of the obstacle in the same manner as described for using handlines in paragraphs 13-26 through 13-29, page 327. It is then tensioned and anchored on the near side of the obstacle. A rope bridge may be built many ways depending upon the tactical situation and area to be crossed. However, all rope bridges share common safety principles for construction and use. Rope bridges must be tensioned as low as practical on the anchor while still facilitating suspending loads and off-loading them. The creation of artificial height (covered later) can be used for rope bridges. The type and location of the tensioning system depend on terrain and situation. METHODS OF TENSIONING 16-4. There are

while still facilitating suspending loads and off-loading them. The creation of artificial height (covered later) can be used for rope bridges. The type and location of the tensioning system depend on terrain and situation. METHODS OF TENSIONING 16-4. There are multiple ways to apply tension to a rope. The method selected depends on the length of the bridge, equipment available, personnel available, and time. Regardless of the method used, the principle remains the same; apply just enough tension to facilitate ease of crossing through the terrain. WARNING Ropes must not be overtensioned. An overtensioned rope is in its weakest state, and the system can apply exponential forces during use. Critical failures can occur with overtensioned ropes. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 371

A rope bridge constructed with a single rope has the risk of critical failure due to cutting and lacks redundancy. A redundancy (in rigging) is the condition in which a rope system will not fail as the result of any single component of the system failing. If the risk or critical nature of the load requires an additional level of redundancy, a second rope bridge may be constructed parallel to the first one. failing. If the risk or critical nature of the load requires an additional level of redundancy, a second rope bridge may be constructed parallel to the first one. Examples of critical loads are a casualty, Soldiers crossing a rope bridge that is high off the ground, and a dry river crossing where a separate belay rope is not used. If two ropes are used, they should be as close as possible so that a single carabiner can be clipped to both lines. An individual would attach to both ropes when crossing, thus having a backup in case of failure. Redundancy is not always necessary or practical but is typically used in training as a risk management tool. METHODS OF CROSSING 16-14. Methods of dry crossings using rope bridges is determined by several factors: * The load being transported on the rope bridge (such as personnel, equipment, and litter). * The risk of the terrain (such as fast-moving water and catastrophic falls). * The angle of the rope bridge (such as level, ascending, and descending). * Equipment available (such as extra ropes, harnesses, and rigging equipment). 16-15. For example, the method chosen for moving a light element with no sustainment gear across a 10-foot stream is different from the method chosen for moving crew-served weapons across a 50-foot-wide, fast-moving river. 16-16. Soldiers lie on top of the rope with a foot hooked on the rope and a knee bent, o positioned nearly in line with the buttocks; the other leg hangs straight to maintain balance. They progress by pulling with their arms. To recover if they fall over, Soldiers hook one leg and the opposite arm over the rope, and then push down with the other hand to regain position. A high line is a type of suspended rope bridge used to transport equipment or casualties high above difficult terrain that might otherwise be impassable. These can be used for personnel movement as well, although this is less common. The high line is used over large rivers, ravines, chasms, or diagonally from the top of a cliff to the ground below. The system may be established on different planes, varying from horizontal to near vertical. High lines keep the load suspended above the terrain as it travels directly between the nearand far-side anchors. 16-34. High lines come with a high level of risk due to the height of the load above the ground. High lines used for personnel movement require careful calculation to ensure system failure will not occur, resulting in catastrophic fall injury. They should only be constructed by advanced or master military mountaineers who have been formally trained in high-line construction for this purpose. SITE SELECTION

movement require careful calculation to ensure system failure will not occur, resulting in catastrophic fall injury. Appendix A Climbing Route Classification The most important tools for risk management in the mountains are route selection and evaluation. Accurately evaluating and selecting routes in high consequence terrain requires a well-developed understanding of technical route classification systems and experience climbing the terrain they describe. Route classifications allow military mountaineers to identify appropriate routes for their Soldiers' skill levels and the technical rope systems required to move on them safely. Misunderstanding or miscommunicating route difficulty can place the life of the mountaineer or the lives of the Soldiers they lead in danger. The U.S. military does not have its own technical route classification systems. Therefore, military mountaineers must use those developed for civilian mountaineering. The classifications discussed in this chapter breakdown and describe the difficulty associated with routes in various types of terrain. Understanding them provides military mountaineers with the base from which to build route identification and selection experience. ROCK CLIMBING CLASSIFICATIONS A-1. There are several systems for classifying different aspects of rock-climbing difficulty. Different types of climbing require different classifications. Also, skill is not the only factor involved in classifying difficulty. The amount of time and effort necessary to complete a climbing route is often more important than

different aspects of rock-climbing difficulty. Different types of climbing require different classifications. Also, skill is not the only factor involved in classifying difficulty. The amount of time and effort necessary to complete a climbing route is often more important than what the hardest move on it is. Depending on the type of route being planned, one or all these route difficulty systems should be considered. YOSEMITE DECIMAL SYSTEM A-2. In North America, the YDS is used to rate the difficulty of rock-climbing routes. It categorizes terrain according to the techniques and physical difficulties encountered when rock climbing. The YDS classes are- * Class 1-hiking. * Class 2-off-trail scramble with the occasional use of hands. * Class 3-moderate scrambling, with short steps of easy climbing. Ropes may be used for beginners, but a guide can often manage the terrain with good coaching and modeling. * Class 4-simple climbing, with exposure. A rope is often used. A fall could be fatal. * Class 5-rock climbing. Usually requires climbers to rope up, belay, and place protection to protect the leader from a long fall. A-3. Class 5 is further subdivided to rate the difficulty of the climbing. The YDS only rates the hardest

Class 5-rock climbing. Usually requires climbers to rope up, belay, and place protection to protect the leader from a long fall. A-3. Class 5 is further subdivided to rate the difficulty of the climbing. The YDS only rates the hardest move on a pitch and does not account for strenuousness, difficulty of placing protection, or quality of the protection: * Class 5.0 to 5.4-easy. This is the simplest form of free climbing. Hands are necessary to support balance. Easy for experienced climbers. * Class 5.5 to 5.6-intermediate. Often no more physically difficult than easier climbing but requires trusting friction and smaller holds. The climber can experience vertical position or overhangs where there are positive holds that require moderate levels of energy expenditure. * Class 5.7 to 5.8-moderate. Considerable climbing experience is necessary. Longer stretches of climbing requiring several points of intermediate protection. Climbing often requires specific techniques, such as jamming, liebacks, or mantles. * Class 5.9 to 5.10-hard. Requires well above average ability and excellent condition. Exposed positions, often combined with small belay points. Passages of the difficult sections can often be accomplished under good conditions. Often combined with aid climbing. * Class 5.11 to 5.15-very difficult. Requires more climbing

above average ability and excellent condition. Exposed positions, often combined with small belay points. Passages of the difficult sections can often be accomplished under good conditions. Often combined with aid climbing. * Class 5.11 to 5.15-very difficult. Requires more climbing ability, experience, and energy expenditure. Each pitch may require several hours to lead. There will only be a few pieces of gear in the pitch capable of holding a fall, with potential falls of 15 to 20 meters. These falls, however, are usually clean and might not cause serious bodily harm. * A4--Serious aid. Most placements will hold only body weight. There may only be a few solid pieces in a pitch. Falls can be 25 to 30 meters, with bad landings and risk of serious injury. * A5-Extreme aid. All placements can hold only body weight. Usually, no protection placed on the entire route can be trusted to stop a fall. CLIMBING COMMITMENT GRADE A-8. Commitment grades (National Climbing Classification System) inform the climber of the approximate time a climber trained to the level of the climb will take to complete the route: * I-several hours. * II-half of a day for the technical portion of the route. * III-most of the day for the technical climbing, any difficulty. * IV-long, full day of climbing. Hardest pitch rated 5.7 YDS or harder. * V-requires at least a day and a half to complete the technical portion of the route, with the hardest pitch rated at 5.8 or harder. Requires a planned bivouac on the route for most teams. * VI-longer than 2 days. Big wall-style climbing, often with extensive aid climbing, hauling of equipment, and supplies for many days on the wall. INTERNATIONAL RATINGS A-9. Climbing difficulties are rated by different systems in other parts of the world. There are countless systems in use, and even within these systems, there are regional variations in the ratings. All ratings are highly subjective. When traveling and climbing, local guidebooks include charts that compare rating systems. 386 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Climbing Route Classification ICE CLIMBING CLASSIFICATIONS A-10. Ice formations change from year to year and throughout the season, causing their difficulty rating to fluctuate. However, they generally form in the same areas and with the same steepness as the underlying features that they build on. Ice climbing ratings have technical and commitment ratings. The numerical ratings are often prefaced with waterfall ice, alpine ice, or mixed rock and ice. A-11. Technical difficulty ratings are as follows: * 1-a frozen lake or streambed. * 2-a pitch with short sections of ice up to 80°; lots of opportunity for protection and good anchors. * 3-sustained ice up to 80°; the ice is usually good, with places to rest, but it requires skill at placing protection and setting anchors. * 4-a sustained pitch that is vertical or slightly less than vertical; may have special features, such as chandeliers and run-outs between protection. * 5-a long, strenuous pitch, possibly 50 meters of 85° to 90° ice, with few, if any, rests between anchors. The pitch may be shorter but on featureless ice. Good skills at placing protection are required. * 6-a full 50-meter pitch of dead vertical ice, possibly of poor quality; requires efficiency

Good skills at placing protection are required. * 6-a full 50-meter pitch of dead vertical ice, possibly of poor quality; requires efficiency of movement and ability to place protection while in awkward stances. * 7-a full-rope length of thin vertical or overhanging ice of dubious adhesion. An extremely tough pitch, physically and mentally, requiring agility and creativity. * 8-simply the hardest ice climbing ever done; extremely bold and gymnastic. A-12. Commitment ratings are as follows: * I-a short, easy climb near the road, with no avalanche hazard and a straightforward descent. * II-a route of one or two pitches within a short distance of rescue assistance, with little objective hazard. * III-a multipitch route at low elevation or a one-pitch climb with an approach that takes about an hour. Appendix B GUIDEBOOKS B-11. A guidebook is a publication containing detailed climbing routes and approach route information. Current local guidebooks are still the most comprehensive and useful tool for gathering information on a specific climbing route or mountain. They contain detailed instructions for getting to these remote areas including the approach to the climb or trailhead. They contain invaluable route information and are readily available for most established mountaineering training areas. LOCAL CLIMBING ORGANIZATIONS B-12. When information is not readily available in guidebooks (such as when training overseas), it may be beneficial to contact a local climbing organization in the area. These organizations exist all over the world even in the most remote and unlikely locations. The local community can provide some of the most accurate and current information that may not be available anywhere else. U.S. GOVERNMENT LAND MANAGEMENT AGENCIES B-13. The U.S. government manages millions of acres of public lands that are excellent training venues for military mountaineering training. Generally, most training areas are managed by the Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, or U.S. Forest Service. training event. SECTION III - TIME-DISTANCE ESTIMATION B-15. The time-distance method covered in chapter 7, table 7-2, page 148 is useful but very general. The Munter method described below affords planners more options to enhance their time-to-distance estimate. THE MUNTER METHOD B-16. The Munter method is an accurate method of calculating route times during planning. It is the most accepted time-distance formula used by mountain professionals and guides. The Munter method combines map distance (kilometers) and elevation change (meters) into a unit of time (hours), then it is divided by an estimated movement rate (kilometers per hour) using various terrain conditions. This method allows the user the ability to break the movement up into different legs and account for different modes of travel. This method is simple to calculate and allows the planner increased flexibility to account for the various paces, changes in elevation, increased loads, and environmental conditions that exist in mountainous terrain. Glossary *bolt A type of rock protection or anchoring component comprised of an expansion bolt or glue-in shaft attached to a hanger to which a carabiner can be attached. *brake strand The strand of a rope system that controls the rate at which a load is lowered or a rappeller descends. carabiner A D-shaped or oval-shaped metal link, with one spring-hinged side, that is used in mountaineering as a connector between soft materials and to capture a freely running rope. *cold-weather injury Any preventable injury resulting from exposure to cold environmental conditions. *coil A secure configuration of rope that allows for easy transport without tangling. couloir Narrow snow- or ice-filled gully. dynamic rope Kernmantle rope designed to stretch and absorb force, primarily used to protect climbers from fall injuries. fall protection Any anchor clipped to a running rope used in belay systems that limits the distance a roped climber falls, should a fall occur. friction hitch A type of hitch tied with webbing or cordage around a rope that can be moved easily while no force is applied to it but cinches and becomes fixed when tensioned. guidebook A publication containing detailed climbing routes and approach route information. gully A
